The Paradoxes of Delusion: Wittgenstein, Schreber, and the schizophrenic mind by Louis A Sass. Published by Cornell University Press, Ithaca and London, 1994; 177 pages; £ 19.50.

John Heaton

John Heaton

London

John Heaton  

Delusions in both psychiatry and psychoanalysis are usually thought of as being some sort of false belief about external reality. Psychoanalysts tend to think of them as due to regression to the wish-fulfilling fantasising of early infancy. So delusions are taken to be due to a break-down in reality testing. It is assumed that babies are out of touch with reality. The problem therefore becomes one of accounting for the gradual development of accurate reality testing, of how a child learns to differentiate truth from illusion and why this developmental process breaks down in schizophrenia.

Sass argues that this way of posing the problem is misguided and due to psychiatrists and psychoanalysts unconsciously assuming the beliefs of enlightenment rationalism. This form of rationalism rigidly divides form from content. It is assumed that the content of the delusion is unrealistic, it is a false belief; but that the form or ‘feel’ or way of belief is essentially normal, or rather like that of the ordinary adult.

Sass uses examples from Schreber's Memoirs and his own practice to show that schizophrenics usually do not experience their delusions as being literally true, but are aware that they are in some sense the products of their own consciousness. Delusions then are not mistaken beliefs about external reality. Rather they are imaginative pictures or representations, a mode of what Wittgenstein has termed ‘seeing-as’, which is neither a percept nor a concept but something added on to a percept. For example I may perceive a cloud but then see it as a donkey floating in the sky.

But whereas the ordinary person can switch in and out of seeing-as, the schizophrenic is locked into it. He has been overcome by the metaphysical vision of solipsism in which other people are experienced as but figments of the solipsist's own conscious activity. Wittgenstein spoke of solipsism as ‘a serious and deep-seated disease of language’ and explored it with great subtlety. Sass uses his work to throw light on delusions.

Clinical Interaction and the Analysis of Meaning: a new psychoanalytic theory by Theodore L Dorpat and Michael L Miller; Published by The Analytic Press, London, 1993; 326 pages; £35.00.

David Smith

David Smith

David Smith  

This book contains two distinct strands. In the first instance it attempts to reformulate psychoanalytic theory in light of recent work on the interactional dynamics of the psychoanalytic situation in the tradition of Langs, Gill and in this country Casement. Dorpat and Miller argue that there are no such things as unconscious phantasy/memory constellations, and that analysts who formulate interpretations in such terms are barking up the wrong tree. The authors state that the unconscious part of the mind engages in a process of analysing the meaning of here-and-now situations, which they call ‘meaning analysis’. To their great credit, Dorpat and Miller make the point that one cannot blithely incorporate unconscious meaning analysis into a traditional psychoanalytic model alongside transference, unconscious phantasy, and so on. One must make a choice. British analysts such as Joseph, Little and Casement have, in my opinion, fudged this issue.

The second strand of the book is to reconceptualise psychoanalytic clinical concepts in the light of notions borrowed from cognitive psychology. Although this is an honourable attempt to bring psychoanalysis into the twentieth century, the way that the authors pursue it sometimes blunts the radical edge of the book. For example, it seems at first that Dorpat and Miller are going to throw out the concept of transference entirely, but in the end they just reconceptualise it along cognitive psychological lines. By the same token, the role played by unconscious phantasy in the traditional model is occupied by 'unconscious pathogenic belief (a term borrowed from Weiss and Sampson) in the new theory. The two concepts seem to me to be interchangeable for all practical purposes.

The strongest aspect of this book is the attempt to frame a more adequate psychological theory to underpin psychoanalytic clinical practice. I must confess to strong reservations about how the authors pursue their aim. In particular, I am concerned that there is little or no discussion of the evidential justification of their theory. How might it be corroborated? How might it be falsified? What is the logical relationship between its theoretical terms and clinical observations? These are vital questions to be asked of any psychoanalytic theory.

Alan Lidmila

Alan Lidmila

Sheffield

Alan Lidmila  

In some ways this book is concerned with the uses of play and language in psychotherapy. Arguably, all psychotherapy, at least of an analytic variety, is concerned with play and language and various, sometimes antagonistic schools of therapy reflect different ways of describing language and play. The editors of this volume are particularly interested in the application of ideas and techniques in working with more than averagely disturbed individuals, often in institutionalised settings. Whilst many of us might agree that exploratory therapy rests within language, and that some of our technique is play in the Winnicottian sense we might also agree that greater disturbance in the patient calls for greater creativity in the therapist. This in turn gives rise to an interesting debate as to the limits and boundaries that may be necessary for therapy to take place. When is a ‘frame deviation’ inspired, creative therapy or wild analysis, something acted upon in the counter-transference? Certain names are then bandied around as examples either of giftedness or madness.

This text owes an explicit acknowledgement to both a Jungian and Freudian strain in analytic thinking. There will be much to please followers of Bettelheim and his classic text in this area (The Uses of Enchantment) because this book is also interested in the meaning and application of, say, Peter Pan in working with adults. However, the authors are also devotees of a perspective that is altogether more Jungian. So, again, people interested in myth, narrative and archetypes will find much to enjoy.

There are two main points of interest to the practitioner; the ways that fairy tales may be analysed and the use of such analysis through technique, especially with disturbed individuals. The reader will encounter many old favourites and possibly some less familiar characters: Wassilissa (about the good-bad mother and separationanxiety), Little Black Sambo (about transitional objects), Briar Rose, Cinderella (not again!) and Peter Pan. I have to say that as someone fairly interested in this area it is already quite well ploughed ground and I am not sure the authors take us anywhere new.

Childhood Adversity and Adult Defence Style in Eating Disorder Patients - A Controlled Study

Ulike Schmidt Gaynor Slone, Jane Tiller Janet Treasure

The aims of the study were (1) to compare the defence style of patients with anorexia nervosa with that of patients with bulimia nervosa and of female controls; (2) to establish whether a link exists between childhood adversity and adult defence style in eating disorder patients. Twenty-six patients with restricting anorexia nervosa (RAN), 61 patients with bulimia nervosa (BN), 37 patients with bulimic anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa with a history of anorexia nervosa (BAN/BN-HistAN) and 88 female controls were given the short Defence Style questionnaire (Andrews, Pollock & Stewart 1989). Eating disorder patients were asked about their childhood care using a semi-structured interview (Harris, Brown & Bifulco 1986). Bulimia nervosa patients had a significantly less mature defence style than the other groups and like the BAN/BN-HistAN group more immature defences than the control group. In the RAN group no childhood predictors of adult defence style were found, whereas in bulimia nervosa, excessive parental control during childhood was a negative predictor of mature defences and physical abuse a positive predictor of immature defence style. These results provide some evidence that childhood adversity may constitute a vulnerability factor for the later development of bulimia nervosa, mediated by personality development.

Kevin Power

Kevin Power

London

Kevin Power  

The purpose of this book is to ‘present the reader with a practical insight into the group-analytic method of group psychotherapy’. It achieves this aim well while avoiding the pitfalls of an instructional manual. All group therapists, trainees and other professionals working with groups will be able to gain much from reading and reflecting on this volume's contents.

The meat of the book is in eight ‘group situations’, each described near the start of the volume. Over thirty practitioners of group-analysis responded to a request to read each of the situations and explain how they would react to each and to explain their interventions. Most of these situations will be instantly recognised by all practitioners - except the last, on the threat of actual violence - hopefully only a rare experience. Each chapter deals with one of these situations and starts with the author of the chapter outlining how the situation challenges the conductor and specifying the tasks and problems. Each introduction is followed by an examination of how a selection of the responding therapists reacted to the situation together with their reasons. There are further chapters on interventions; establishing and maintaining a therapeutic environment; interpretation: why, for whom and when; and a chapter of conclusions. An appendix provides a brief overview of other analytically-oriented group therapeutic approaches. All this makes for absorbing reading, especially when you have previously made your own hypothetical interventions on paper.

For it is intended that the reader should respond to all situations her/himself, stating for each what the situation is understood to be about, what intervention, if any, would be made and lastly, giving briefly the reasons for having made such an intervention. It is a most useful activity - interesting to compare what one has written with what the thirty respondents provided, and with the encompassing remarks of the writer of the chapter concerned. The variety of response was quite wide in each situation, with the personality of the respondent sometimes rather predominating over the usefulness of the response itself to the member or group concerned.

Commentary by a Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist

Evelyn Katz

Evelyn Katz

Associate Member, British Association of Psychotherapists

Evelyn Katz  

In this case study, the patient sought therapy because of an overwhelming sense of failure in both his emotional and professional life. The clinical material provided ends with the patient's assertion that despite the work of the session, he ‘feels empty’. Perhaps the therapeutic interaction reflects this sense of failure and, as such, is a re-enactment in the transference of the relationship between a well-meaning but unavailable internal mother and a child who, possibly, cannot make use of what such a mother has to offer. In addition, there are hints of narcissistic strivings which fail in their attempts to overcome some earlier failure in his primary relationships.

Efforts to understand the patient's internal world have made me think about the paucity of background information available. We are told that he is the youngest of three children of a professional couple, and that his marriage to an older, successful career woman has disintegrated. The absence of much biographical detail invokes many questions - about the sex of his siblings, the nature of the parents' professions, the reason for the seven year gap before the birth of the patient, and about an apparently ‘absent’ father. The patient remembers that he was often sent on residential holiday schemes during school vacations. This memory made me reflect on whether he was the child of an older mother absorbed in her own career, and on how this may relate to the patient's feeling that she was a well-intentioned but inept mother who got rid of him during holiday times because she was ‘unable to know what to do with him’. Curiosity, suggesting a lively, interested mind, appears to be absent from the patient and is projected into external objects - in this case the reader.

From the information provided it seems probable that the patient is someone who inhabits an impoverished internal world, with objects who may have been in touch with him concretely rather than emotionally. This is reflected in the scant history provided, the lack of curiosity, the difficulty in attaching meaning to his experiences both to the past and in the present, and in his apparent lack of potency. Evidence of the therapist's difficulty in establishing contact, particularly during the first six months of therapy, made me think further about a patient who is in projective identification with an impermeable, distancing and distant object, like a mother unable to contain her child's projections. We are told of his constant talking, explaining and theorising, which is used not for reflection but to keep his therapist at a distance, while she feels unable to ‘touch him’ with her interpretations. Through projective identification he communicates his extreme fragility and vulnerability, and the therapist feels that interpretations have to be perfectly timed, and perhaps carefully worded, for them to be allowed in. At times, the therapist abandons the patient in favour of organising her own mind and, as such, might represent both a narcissistic maternal object and a mutually exclusive parental couple from whom the patient perhaps feels unbearably excluded.

Jung and Searles: a comparative study by David Sedgwick. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 1993; 178 pages; £30.00 (hardback).

Fiona Ross

Fiona Ross

London

Fiona Ross  

Deceptively small, this dense, informative and carefully written book has the dual aims of contrasting the work of Jung and Searles and of forming a unified theory of psychotherapy from their ideas.

The writer, himself a Jungian analyst, identifies Searles as the psychoanalyst who has most to offer to analytical psychology. The writings of Jung and Searles are then explored as complementary in tension and as dissonant. The centre of focus is initially on their two theoretical positions and then on the areas of psychopathology, psychotherapy and lastly on the therapist him/herself.

Both theorists are shown to have drawn from their own inner world experiences, having brushed closely enough with psychosis to allow them to see pathology as potential and to appreciate the importance of the therapist's personality in defining the limits of therapy. They are seen as in agreement on the fundamentally unconscious quality of human nature, the need not only to see the presenting individual in depth, but in a scope that can link the ancestral with the teleological: for Jung, a dimension in his exploration of the numinous, for Searles, the backdrop of psychotherapy and clinical experience.

Sedgwick looks at the pluralistic phenomenology of both theorists in their peopling of the unconscious. He compares Jung's concept of complexes (which can be personified) with Searles' ‘multiple identity processes’. Again the key difference is seen in Jung's archetypal versus Searles' personalistic view of their sources. Both forsake the medical model and see psychopathology in terms of the frequent interference of multiple inner selves and the failure of consciousness to understand them, leaving the individual persistently unconscious of him/herself. There is a difference in how the painful or conflictual events which give rise to defensively unassimilated emotional reactions or pathogenic introjects are seen as originating. For Searles they arise within the context of the immediate family, for Jung their source is any affective relationship, personal or impersonal. Consistent with this difference, Sedgwick describes the greater emphasis in Searles' theoretical and clinical models on the transference and on transference interpretations, whereas Jung is informed more strongly by the symbolic and particularly by manifestations of the collective unconscious. Both clinicians look to individualism as the path rather than the goal but to Jung it means discovery of preconscious, preexistent wholeness, the bedrock of imaginal activity, whereas to Searles it is the personal, the journey from symbiosis to separation from the mother.

Dorothy Judd  

This book attempts to look at the psychological, psychosocial and behavioural aspects of cancer. Much of the discourse is given weight by encompassing a range of research and frequent references to the literature. It has many good, common-sense approaches and understandings, of which this gives a flavour (p. xvi):

The most important one [fact] …is given to us by the patient himself. He shares with us a dramatic moment, of extreme emotional intensity. To train oneself in ‘psycho-oncology’ is perhaps to explore one's own limits, and above all to be prepared to listen to patients and to comprehend their distress, before, possibly, knowing what to do to help them.

However, the foregoing thoughtful example, of a reference to ‘one's own limits’, which could imply an attempt to be aware of the impact and meaning for us, the worker, (and ultimately, I think, could mean to pay attention to the countertransference and to projective mechanisms) is not developed or maintained throughout the book. That makes it unsatisfactory for me although I think it would be a useful resource for clinicians in a general overview way. It may also be useful, in a factual ‘do-it-yourself’ way, for people with cancer.

There is an interesting chapter which briefly traces the history of approaches to cancer over the centuries wherein ‘loss’ and ‘lack’ seem to underlie a predisposition to cancer (p. 2):

To surmount the loss, the patient appears to have denied suffering so as to hyperadapt to reality, to the detriment of his emotional life.

Indeed, there are many interesting examples of the issues which arise in a debate on the psychogenic approach, such as Greer and Morris (1975) successfully predicting the result of breast lump biopsies on the basis of a psychological questionnaire. They found that the rate of malignancy was inversely proportional to the capacity to express aggression. However, these findings are not conclusive for there is other research which points to emotion not influencing malignancies.

London

Dorothy Judd  

The competent book, which arises out of a conference in 1990, would be of interest to psychologists, psychiatrists, psychotherapists, general practitioners, nurses and doctors. Many of the treatments described are not widely available as they arise out of research settings. One of the main themes which emerges is the importance of early detection of people with physical illness at high risk of developing psychological problems. The editors suggest that hospital doctors, general practitioners and nurses can be trained to pick out those patients who need to be referred to psychiatrists or psychotherapists.

Christopher Dare's chapter serves as good introduction to the whole area of considering different theoretical approaches. He explains psychotherapeutic theories of psychosomatic disorders with a specific focus on eating disorders. He lucidly traces the development of psychological disorder presenting as somatic disorder - in other words, conversion hysteria and the subsequent search for the meaning of a physical symptom without necessarily bringing about any cure. Dare explains how the development of object relations theory and the use of the transference has informed, influenced and enriched this approach.

Jane Bunster  

On reading this session and its introduction, the most striking feature that came to my mind was the patient's controlledness and consequent difficulty in taking in and digesting any attempted interpretive comments from the therapist. Two examples of this are firstly in the introduction when the writer describes his reaction to the interpretations ‘as though they were simply an interruption in his chain of thought’ and secondly, in the session itself when the therapist felt put down by the patient's response, ‘yes, there is something in that, but I want to get back to X’.

In thinking about how to conceptualise this feature of control which is not at all uncommon, I have found Dr Michael Fordham's theory of the original self and the process of deintegrative-reintegrative sequences which form the basis of a two-person relationship of great help and interest. I would also bear in mind examples from my infant observation studies particularly with regard to feeding sequences.

Dr Michael Fordham's theory of the Original Self is a development of Jung's idea of the Self (often with a capital S so that it is distinguished from the more ego-based sense of self - little s). Jung postulates the Self as a ‘psychic totality which includes inherited dispositions, archetypal expectations, closely related to instincts and the potential for wholeness which is unique to every individual’. Whereas Jung thought of ‘individuation’ as a process related to the latter half of one's life, when ego-oriented tasks such as success in work and supporting and raising a family become less pressing, Dr Fordham postulated the theory that individuation starts from the beginning of life. The infant (or foetus) is an unique original Self, undifferentiated but including every archetypal potential for growth. One of these archetypal potentials is to unfold from the self and move out to the external world and have the expectation of meeting something ‘out there’. Most obvious is the expectation to meet a nipple and breast which will nourish the baby and help him grow. To describe this process, Fordham coined the word ‘deintegrate’. Also the movement of smacking lips, sucking fingers, is related to this process as may be the similar movements which can be seen in utero, as also the taking in of amniotic fluid. Hopefully this unfolding or deintegration is sufficiently well met and received, so let us say the baby receives a satisfactory feed. He then reintegrates the experience and settles into a refreshing and recreative sleep - hence our development throughout life really consists of deintegrative and reintegrative sequences, the foundations of which are laid in early infancy and which we then build on throughout life. Another analogy we can use is breathing in and out. If, for whatever reason, these deintegrative moves are not well enough met or not met at all, a state of disintegration may occur and, if this is too frequent or too long experienced, a defence pathology of the self may develop and the child or adult remains with a well-defined fortress from which no deintegrative moves unfold. This is at some cost as there is no opportunity for any inner-world development, fantasy or imaginative symbolism, or relationship to an inner or outer object. This creates a sense of emptiness inside with no introjected constant object.

While always welcoming candidates not just from the so-called ‘core professions’ but from a wide range of disciplines, the profession of psychotherapy is itself largely untouched by other disciplines. In few trainings, it would seem, is there much time for the study of texts outside of the clinical canon while the professional culture in general often seems to be curiously cut off from the wider world of ideas. International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 75, 469, 1994

The Feminine Self and Penis Envy

Marita Torsti

This paper examines the integrative role of inner genitality in the formation of penis internalisations, which form part of the feminine self. Penis envy, operating simultaneously with the anxiety arising from a realisation of the introitus under the influence of inner genitality, organises functioning inner and outer female penis structures. This three-dimensionality of inner genitality, penis envy and anxiety for penetration is the condition of a functioning femininity. In the light of an analytic case history, the author follows the thawing out of a phallic defence position and the awakening of the obstructed genitality. Phallicity is seen as a traumatic defence structure, which prevents the development of functioning penis identifications. In the phallic mental world, the penis takes on an idealised and concrete meaning. Its desirability is denied, and the woman excludes her inner genitality from her relationship to it as an object. When most obstructed in her womanhood, a woman becomes a phallus herself. She lives in an imitative identity, in which the internalising psychic functions have come to a standstill. In such a mind, the ultimate purpose of defence is to avoid annihilation anxiety.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Vol. 75, 499, 1994

Paradise Lost: A Case of Hysteria Illustrating a Specific Dynamic of Seduction Trauma

Abby Adams-Silvan and Mark Silvan

This paper presents extensive clinical data illustrating the case of a middle-aged woman, who as a child participated in an extended sexual relationship with her elder brother. The patient suffered from an hysterical personality disorder with somatic distress and a compulsion to repeat disastrous social and work situations. In her treatment, the patient re-enacted the seduction and subsequent experience in various ways. The analysis and understanding of her symptoms, social problems and re-enactments in the transference strongly suggested that the trauma of her seduction was the result of the loss of precociously stimulated and experienced pleasure rather than loss of impulse control. The compulsion to repeat apparently represented the wish not only to master, but the desire to return to the pleasure of the experience as a true compromise formation. Although many other dynamics were of course operative, interpretations of her wish to recreate the lost pleasures were most helpful.

Ruth Berkowitz  

This is a book about psychotherapy, written essentially for members of the medical profession, from medical student to consultant. It is an attempt to convey information

322

to the audience about a range of approaches to patients with emotional problems, including psychoanalytic, systemic, group, behavioural and cognitive. It is also an effort to communicate to doctors the importance of understanding the role of emotional and psychological factors in their work.

The book, although divided into ten chapters, seems to be in two main sections. The first section is concerned with a psycho-analytic or psychodynamic approach to therapy and starts with an introduction to psychoanalytic theory and technique. These chapters are well written and interesting although there is some overlap. The impression conveyed by the writers of this section is that they have given considerable thought to the main purpose of the book. That is, how can medical doctors in different settings, having in general a model of diagnosis and cure, be enabled to take an interest in psychotherapy and what might they want to know, e.g. what is psychotherapy, why should they be interested in it, and how might it be integrated into their work? There is reference to the work of the Balints who have obviously made an important contribution to this way of thinking.

There are, in what I have called this first section, some guidelines for the assessment of the suitability of patients for psychodynamic psychotherapy which are very helpful, although I am not sure that there would be unanimous agreement about the view of two of the authors that patients with psychosomatic problems are unsuitable. While the initial chapters focus on the issue of patients requiring referral to a psychotherapist, the emphasis in some of the later chapters in this section tends to be more on the integration of psychotherapeutic skills into the doctor's own practice. This may require integration of models, medical and psychotherapeutic, as well as the integration of ideas about mind and body.

London

John Hill  

A curious first impression of this book is the ambiguity of authorship and title. Ostensibly there are two authors, yet in his very clear and useful foreword John Steiner refers repeatedly to ‘the author’, in the singular, from which one gathers he means Murray Jackson. In the preface Murray Jackson describes how Paul Williams, a trained anthropologist, was appointed as a ‘participant observer’ to Jackson's ward

310

at the Maudsley Hospital, making many video and audio tape recordings of the work there. Later, Williams suggested these might form the basis of a book, which he eventually edited once it was in a manuscript form written, presumably, by Murray Jackson.

The main title is also misleading since the storms described turn out to be not only clearly imaginable but, as the contradictory sub-title implies, full of accessible meaning. Towards the end a partial explanation is given in the assertion that some psychotics show ‘a quality of existence that is difficult if not impossible for the more sane person to imagine’. In thus superficially presenting itself as uncertain both of its origin and identity the book introduces something of the quandary life poses for the patients it describes.

The bulk of the book consists of seven ‘clinical vignettes’ of patients in the former Ward 6 of the Maudsley Hospital. This ward was rare, if not unique, in applying a psycho-analytic perspective to the treatment of the severely disturbed within a general psychiatric context. Aged between 25 and 30 at the initiation of their treatment, the patients were followed up for some years after discharge. Recordings were made both of patient interviews (usually observed by others through a one-way screen) and of subsequent staff discussion. Excerpts from these are given at length and in detail. The main interviewer and discussant is Murray Jackson.

What emerges most strikingly is Jackson's basic method of work, which is essentially that of translating a psychotic presentation into a sane form. He does not, of course, always get it right, but when he does the examples have great dramatic impact and can result in a sudden, if temporary, return to sanity for the patient.

Robert Tollemache  

Books on psychoanalytic work with adolescents are rare so this book deserves attention for this reason before even thinking about its contents. It is also important because it is a book in the Kleinian tradition about adolescence, and furthermore because it describes the work of the adolescent department of the Tavistock Clinic, one of the main centres of psychoanalytic work with adolescents in the UK.

There are three main sections. One examines in depth three works of art, Romeo and Juliet and Much Ado about Nothing by Shakespeare, and Eugene Onegin by Pushkin.. The second deals with psychoanalytic theory in relation to adolescence, while the third gives extensive case illustrations of work with young people and in some cases with their families too.

The first is the most purely pleasurable one. The personal interpretations of the plays offer new and refreshing insights, which one might not always agree with but which are always stimulating. Perhaps the basic message the author has for us about Romeo and Juliet is that the conflict-ridden state of Verona, and the warring adolescent gangs that destroy the peace of the city with their lawlessness, illustrate the splitting and projection involved in the paranoid/schizoid position. Romeo and Juliet's tragedy is that they seek but fail to move on into the depressive position.

In Much Ado, Copley suggests, that unlike Verona, Messina and the adolescent group that Beatrice and Benedict belong to offer a container for the paranoid/schizoid position that Beatrice and Benedict are in at the beginning of the play. They defensively reject love and especially love for each other.

David Smith

David Smith

David Smith  

I write this having just returned from a conference devoted to the academic study of psychoanalysis. On two separate occasions it was suggested that the writings of Adolf Grunbaum be excluded from the curricula of academic courses on psychoanalysis. Out of an audience of over sixty psychoanalytically-orientated academics and students, only one person other than myself expressed disquiet about this proposal.

Neville Singh objects to my endorsement of Griinbaum's views. In particular, he objects to Grunbaum's objections to the hermeneutic approach to psychoanalysis preferred by Habermas, Ricoeur and others. I am far too ignorant about the contributions of Habermas and Ricoeur to offer an opinion about the relative merits of the ‘Grünbaumian’ and hermeneutic interpretations of psychoanalysis. However, I think it important to note that Grunbaum rejects the hermeneutic view in the context of a reasoned argument.

I invite Mr Singh (and others who share his beliefs) to offer a reasoned argument turning on specific philosophical, theoretical or clinical issues to which I (and others who share my beliefs) might respond. Surely this would be preferable to a global dismissal of Grünbaum's work and the attempts by some to place it in the category of ‘forbidden knowledge’.

Liam Clarke has done it again! I don't know why you print his diatribes which are lacking in coherence and really quite ignorant.

London

Jean Thomson  

This is a time when so many of us who read the British Journal of Psychotherapy are aware that the organisational foundations upon which we have based our working lives and our personal lives are shifting almost daily. Social work, education, the NHS

151

are changing from diversely evolving systems of varying kinds of professionalism into organisations with an over-emphasis on the language and ethos of one system, financial management. In learning this new language for our work, we try at the same time to preserve and develop the ideas which have underpinned our various skilled applications. Whether we like it or not, we must all become ‘political’ and play a part in ensuring that the knowledge bases of our various professions continue to be usefully employed. Otherwise there is a real danger that our particular wheel will be harnessed to a runaway cash register.

Into this confusing situation Andrew Samuels makes a bold foray, addressing a varied audience from the very specialised psychotherapist to the general public. He is a Jungian analyst, well known as a lecturer and public speaker as well as a writer. He writes as he speaks - his voice rings out of the pages, confidently asserting that new ways must be found for psychotherapists to understand as well as to influence the socio-political spheres in Western culture. I quote (p.75):

I want to suggest that, rather than looking for psychopathology in culture, which is so easy to find, we try to look with psychopathology, with a psychopathological eye. We should not only search for hidden depression in the culture, or for paranoid projections between nation states, or for the sado-masochistic patterns in pornography. Rather let us see how our own depression makes us regard things in a certain way, through a lens preoccupied with our own destructiveness. Let us see how an envious eye makes us see envy everywhere, making us accept that what is good in modern culture can be rubbished by a weary intelligentsia…. (We should) move outward armed with the tools of the trade, which are not methods, theories and interpretations alone, but also the very symptoms, syndromes, illnesses and problems without which depth psychology would have no social function.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

One section of this issue is taken up with the attempts to apply psychodynamic thinking, and practice, to social phenomena and to the social setting of psychotherapy. There has been a considerable effort, for almost as long as there has been psychoanalysis, to understand society in terms of the psycho-analytic view of what an individual is. A number of our papers here debate aspects of psycho-analytic social psychology. Joseph Berke gives an account of the way that psychotic experiences can be moved between a patient, his therapist and the milieu in which both live. Such a milieu, the therapeutic community, is charged with the task of containing that which is uncontainable by the individual. Samuel Stein describes intolerable experiences in a medical institution when staff are under pressure. That hospital, not consciously designed to withstand those experiences, appears to have created unwittingly a specific style of containing those personal experiences. In consequence at least some individuals suffer consequences which can only be described as ‘pathogenic’. René Kaes is concerned with this fact; the intention to care often gives rise to institutions with an exceedingly uncaring practice. He presents a theoretical formulation of such institutions where individuals work out the unconscious meaning of their impulse to care. He draws on a tradition of psycho-analytic thought about institutions that derives from the South American, José Bleger; unconscious sociability has a deeply depersonalising aspect. Claudio Neri, also part of the continental tradition, bases his views instead on Bion's approach to groups. He organises the life of the group around the idea that the group organism itself has an enduring tradition that determines for better or worse the future of life in the group.

A different kind of application of psycho-analytic views is Anthony Ryle's synthetic brain-child, cognitive analytic therapy. He has tried to fill in the empty clause in cognitive therapy - that it lacks a proper theory of how malfunction arises in an individual patient. He supplies psycho-analytic views about the aetiology in the early life of people who become patients. In this piece he is responding to some comments about his paper published in the Journal last autumn (Vol. 10(1)). He argues strongly for the ‘damage from outside’ theory of causation, and enters the debate that exists so turbulently within psycho-analysis itself at present. The recent revelation of the very high levels of sexual abuse of children strengthens the argument that later psychological morbidity derives from actual damage from outside. As a theory it still has the elegant simplicity and parsimony that attracted Freud to it in his early work with hysterical patients. Lynnett Fraser is careful however to attempt to understand her patient's experience of abuse in terms of the contemporary intrapsychic world of the little girl. Abuse does not occur in a psychic vacuum. Fraser's patient was, at the time of abuse, already struggling with currents of sexual desire and super-ego oppression. It is this colossal task of unravelling these interactions between inner and outer which make simple answers attractive, but which also make more prolonged investigation a fascinating challenge. Unravelling the internal status of sexuality from what is imposed upon the child from without reaches a new level of complexity when we consider sexuality in the transference. David Mann observes that the sexuality which may fill the setting in which our investigations proceed is uncomfortable, and uncomfortable to discuss.

UKCP

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley  

Dear Sir

The members of the Psychoanalytic and Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Section (PPPS) of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy have read with interest the letter from the member organisations of the British Confederation of Psychotherapists in the Winter '93 edition of the Journal.

The PPPS represents 31 organisations, of which 21 are training bodies. In addition to this Section, there are two other Sections in UKCP which are psychoanalyticallybased: the Analytical Psychology Section and the Psychoanalytically-based Therapy with Children Section. Together we represent over 1,500 registered practitioners.

On behalf of the PPPS, I want to draw the attention of your readers to a potential misunderstanding concerning the status of the BCP in relation to the UKCP. The BCP represents a group of psychoanalytic psychotherapy organisations. The UKCP is the umbrella organisation for the profession, including all the major forms of psychotherapy. As the national umbrella body, the UKCP holds the single national seat for the United Kingdom on the Board of the European Association for Psychotherapy, administers the national Register of Psychotherapists, and negotiates for the profession with Government departments.

The PPPS regrets that some organisations believed it necessary to form an organisation separate from the broad stream of psychoanalytic psychotherapy in this country. We await the publication of the aims and criteria of the BCP, to see how these may differ from our own aims, ethical guidelines and training criteria.

Haya Oakley

Chair, Psychoanalytic and Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Section (UKCP)

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 74, Part 5, 1993

Some Reflections on Humour in Psychoanalysis

Ronald Baker

This article proposes that for humour to be effective as a therapeutic intervention is psychoanalytic treatment, it must approximate an affect releasing and growth promoting interpretation. The presence and psychological significance of surprise, which is common to both wit and ‘good’ interpretations are taken as the point of departure and the importance of the psychoanalyst's spontaneity is discussed in relation to this. The author explains his opposition to the use of humour as a contrived communication: as a parameter aimed at reviving a dying analysis or as an attempt to resolve an impasse. In particular the dangers of countertransference acting out and the provision of transference gratifications are explored. Equal emphasis is placed on recommending that the analysis of a patient's humorous responses should not be neglected and how an analyst without humour may negatively affect the treatment process. The paper includes clinical vignettes which illustrate the constructive and creative use of humour in the analytic situation.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 74, Part 5, 1993

The Uniqueness of the Patient-Analyst Pair: Approaches for Elucidating the Analyst's Role

Judy L Kantrowitz

This paper describes ways in which patient-analyst interactions result in a unique creation in each psychoanalytic endeavour. The particular character of the analyst and analysand overlap in a manner that potentially influences both the depth and the limits of the analysis. Analysts, therefore, need to be alert to their impact on the analytic process. Three approaches for elucidating the analyst's role and its effect on the patient are described. Case examples illustrate the impeding effect of unrecognised similarities between patients and analysts. Once the analysts became aware of these similarities, there was a change in their behaviour, resulting in a deepening and expanding of the patients' analytic experiences.

Who Cares

Barrie Buxton

Barrie Buxton

Barrie Buxton  

Dear Editor

As we notice in psychotherapy as the hour draws to its close so the patient begins to be serious. As Bob Hinshelwood begins to say goodbye, so we hear something of racism. Of course, if someone wishes to have a confession, I am quite happy to oblige. I am racially prejudiced. But where I differ from the Editor is in being none too ready in being able to see ‘extraordinary tolerance’ in the Middle Ages or, to the point, in being able to see fault in Western Culture. I am sorry but racial prejudice has nothing to do with points of the compass. The qustion I ask is, ‘Does it matter?’ What is our task if it is not to say. ‘Be who you are, speak who you are, irrespective?’ And where done, to assess those who reply with hatred? Of course, it does not mean that I believe in racial prejudice. But, if you wish to have a world without, you will find the inspiration of that is Western.

Barrie Buxton

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Development, as psychotherapists all know, is hard won. And I can reflect back on ten years of helping the Journal to develop, from the days when it was a worried gleam in the eye to the present when it is established as a central publication for the profession. Those anxious early days were compounded by the number of similar projects that sprouted up at the same time. No-one knew if the profession would take to the written word and write as well as read. Even then we were forced to question ‘market forces’ and wonder how it would deal with us. In this case, of course, it has been a real market - with co-operation as well as merely cut-throat competition. All development has to negotiate that blend of cutting throats with solid and supportive co-operation. Otherwise development becomes polarised as either a frightening set of compulsions and domination; or sentimentalised.

Christina Wieland describes this ambivalence and the phantasies that compose the ‘monstrous underside’ to development and creation in its most stark form - having babies. She is concerned about the denial of the ambivalence towards reproductive technology which is then left, unconsciously, to loom in frightening form behind the obstetric activity. In this area David Mann considers castration anxiety as the developmental anxiety aroused through differences and the wished-for retreat into self-castration which abolishes, supposedly, sexual difference. Vivienne Lewin describes personal development in similar terms, the struggle to develop a separateness. The patients she is concerned with each had a twin. And in each case the twinship provided opportunity to avoid difference by avoiding separateness and its consequences. Because of the inevitable twinning with the therapist an opportunity emerges to win a psychotherapeutic development towards accepting the loneliness of separation.

Nathan Field is concerned to clarify the whole conception of development itself, since so often the category of the undeveloped or ‘primitive’ is conflated with the abnormal and pathological. He traces this confusion to the failure to distinguish properly between the two meanings of normality - the average and the ideal. Herman Daldin in contrast is very clear about the normality that he sees for his patients. It is a functional normality - to be gauged in terms of ego functions. He is concerned with those patients who appear to have become particularly stuck in development and seemingly have entered a blind alley. Such ‘pathologically organised’ patients are very much in vogue currently as the source of new ideas and approaches to psycho-analytic psychotherapeutic work. In contrast with much British work in which the tendency is to focus on ever finer details of the transference and counter-transference, Daldin follows the recommendations of Anna Freud in introducing an initial period of treatment in which interventions are modified from the classical technique in various ways. He introduces us to the notion of ‘developmental help’, therapeutic acts which fill the gaps, at least temporarily, in the patient's ego functioning.

[[RunningHead]]

Cultural Collapse

Rob Weatherill

Rob Weatherill

Rob Weatherill  

Dear Editor

Your readers may be interested to know about the publication this spring of Cultural Collapse by Free Association Books. The book arose out of my background in education and my experience, training and practice in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, but also very much from discussion, debate and argument with colleagues and friends over many years.

It provides a searching study of the growing impoverishment of life in Western society - a subject that has been neglected on the whole by psychoanalysis in recent times. On the one hand, it sets out basic psychoanalytic principles, differentiating psychoanalytic psychotherapy from other forms of psychotherapy; and, on the other hand, it uses these principles to explore in a radical way contemporary issues of violence, addiction, the crisis in the family and education, the loss of our capacity to contain and savour experience, feminism and the shattering of male narcissism, and the unravelling of the social fabric.

The central paradox explored is that while we undoubtedly enjoy greater freedom and abundance than ever before, at least in the rich affluent parts of the world, we nevertheless notice a corresponding inner weakness, rage and loss of cohesion. This psychial depletion parallels and is connected with the depletion of our external resources.

The book reminds us that psychoanalysis is not only arguably our sole coherent theory and treatment of mental illness, but also it is a theory of human nature and the human condition, and is therefore well placed to comment on the problems of modernity. It explains how psychoanalytic ideas have been consistently misunderstood and and overthrown in favour of narcissistic options, which deny essential human vulnerability, relatedness and solidarity as well as the apprehension of universal values.

The explosive force of modern consumer capitalism is seen as excessively stimulating desire, fatally narrowing the gap between impulse and gratification, sponsoring splitting, regression and defusion - necessitating the massive mobilisation of brutal internal controls, paralleled externally, by the growth of totalitarianism, paramilitarism and surveillance.

Motherhood and Sexuality by Marie Langer (translation, introduction and afterword by Nancy Caro Hollander). Published by the Guilford Press, New York and London, 1992; 305 pages; £24.95.

Sheila Ernst

Sheila Ernst

London

Sheila Ernst  

Marie Langer has been, until recently, a hidden heroine for those people in the English-speaking world interested in the connections between psychotherapy and politics. She made the rare attempt to combine the profession of psychoanalyst with political commitment and activism; thus it becomes impossible to read her book outside the context of her life. Like many other psychoanalysts of her generation (she was born in 1910 and died in 1987), she grew up in Vienna and left because of Hitler's persecution of the Jews. What was unusual was that she left to volunteer as a doctor in the Spanish Civil War. She fled from Europe to Argentina and was later a political refugee in Mexico. She built up the Psychoanalytical Institute in Argentina, always stressing the importance of connecting the psychoanalytical perspective with a Marxist understanding and an awareness of the position of women. It was during this period of her life that Motherhood and Sexuality was first published (in 1951). However as the dictatorship in Argentina became more repressive Langer led a group of psychoanalysts who believed that psychoanalysis could not remain neutral and eventually left the International Psychoanalytic Association.

Hysteria by Terry Johnson, Royal Court Theatre, London, Royal Court Writers Series published by Methuen Drama1993.

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner  

When Freud wrote that hysterical symptoms and crises constitute a pantomime of sexual pleasure, he was identifying the way in which an initially psychical affect would pass into bodily expression instead of being verbally spoken about - but he could have been describing Terry Johnson's play Hysteria. The play shifts between serious dialogue and farcical sexual pantomime as Freud's last thoughts, recent memories and suppressed anxieties dictate the action.

Johnson builds on a factually correct meeting between Salvador Dali and Sigmund Freud that took place in July 1938 at Freud's lodgings in Elsworthy Road, and an apparently true incident in which the bewildered surrealist found a bike with a hotwater bottle attached to the saddle in Freud's backyard. The dramatic action is transferred to a brilliant reproduction of Freud's consulting room and today's Freud museum in Maresfield Gardens. The Dali/Freud encounter becomes elaborated through the intervention of a living case history, Jessica, who, as a victim in her own right and the avenging daughter of an abused mother, confronts Freud with his abandonment of the seduction theory.

The play abounds with historical inaccuracies including the implication that Freud is under the effects of the morphine administered by his physician only in September 1939 two days before his death. For, following the injections, the harassed, deathfixated Freud experiences what is hinted to be by the end of the play a recurring guiltridden nightmare. This includes last thoughts about his death and the fate of his sisters left behind in Austria; recent memories on the publication of ‘Moses and Monotheism’, and his own visit to an English theatre farce; and suppressed anxieties about events in 1897 and his shift away from fact in the seduction theory to fantasy and the discovery of infantile sexuality.

The character of Dali (Tim Potter) acts as a foil to the intensity between Jessica and Freud (played by Phoebe Nicholls and Henry Goodman). Dali enters a scene of pantomime and slapstick farce with the comment to Freud: ‘What Dali merely dreams, you live.’ These opening sequences are reminiscent of the distorted and disguised content of dreams where a jumble of memories and associations become superimposed on one another. However as Freud and Jessica speak of the uncovering and reconstruction of the abuse experienced by her mother, Dali through his asides and commentary helps us to digest the unpalatable facts of sexual abuse.

Response to Burgoyne and Harris, the Discussants of ‘A Formal Science for Psychoanalysis’

Robert Langs and Anthony Badalamenti

Anthony Badalamenti

Robert Langs MD, 133 West 72nd Street, Suite 304, New York, NY 10023, USA

Anthony Badalamenti  

We respond to the two discussions of our paper by Bernard Burgoyne and Tirril Harris, not so much to take issue with the unwarranted rejection of our efforts and the erroneous arguments used for this purpose, but primarily because of the grave concern for the fields of psychotherapy and psychoanalysis (we will not distinguish the two here) that these discussion papers aroused in each of us. Their prejudice and evident resistance against the new methods and ideas reflected in these two papers should be cause for deep worry in every psychotherapist regardless of clinical persuasion.

We have little to say about the specific criticisms levelled at our work; they are insubstantial, negatively biased and, often, simply in error. It will do little to argue our position further because, like our discussants, most readers already stand on one side or the other of this debate. We need to step back for a broader perspective.

We are reminded here of Bishop Samuel Wilberforce's critique of Darwin's theory of evolution as expressed in his debate with Thomas Huxley: ‘Was it on your grandmother's or grandfather's side of the family that you descended from the apes?’ asked the Bishop. What possible answer can one make?

None of our results is given serious consideration by either critic and, as such, there can be no fruitful response on our part. In passing we note that our scales which, as one discussant noted after a belaboured bit of carping, have, of course, been utilised quite reliably by three different teams of scorers, do represent real, quantifiable increments; we are not dealing with either metaphor or flight into physics, but with a set of remarkable findings - of great surprise to ourselves and evidently to others - results that we believe call for serious consideration.

The essence of our presentation is that we found that, by quantifying measures of the means or vehicles through which humans communicate, we derived some rather striking laws of human expression and therapeutic communication. As it turned out (and much of this work was a matter of trying out intuitions), the property of human messages that defines whether a patient or therapist (or anyone, for that matter) is in the story telling or intellectualising mode of expression proves to be an ever-present, rather mundane yet exceedingly powerful dimension of human monologues and communicative exchanges - within and outside therapy.

On Kissing, Tickling and Being Bored: psychoanalytic essays on the unexamined life by Adam Phillips. Published by Faber & Faber, London, 1993; 143 pages; £14.99.

Gillian Wilce

Gillian Wilce

London

Gillian Wilce  

A phobia, like a psychoanalytic theory, is a story about where the wild things are.

The bored child is waiting, unconsciously, for an experience of anticipation.

[T]he only way to discover your projects is to notice - to make conscious - what you reckon are the obstacles.

So epigrammatic is the style of these extraordinary essays about ‘the most ordinary things in the world’ that the temptation (not wholly avoided here) is to review them simply by quoting and quoting.

Like the psychoanalysis which most interests Adam Phillips, his book is ‘prodigal in its use of analogy and promiscuous in its references’: on one page a child patient storing up worries to offer as gifts to his mother and on the next the etymology of the word ‘worry’; from Rousseau on being unable to buy the pears he desires to Freud on jokes to George Crabbe on the definition of an obstacle, all within a half-dozen paragraphs. Phillips' own desire in these essays is to ‘circulate’ the language of psychoanalysis ‘in unusual places with other languages’ (literature, for example, and the stories people tell about themselves) in order to illuminate and question both psychoanalysis itself and the most everyday of experiences: why tickling? what does composure mean? what is happening when we are bored? what is the kiss as a thing in itself?

And the experiences and the psychoanalysis, of course, question one another, often with unexpected outcomes. ‘One of the dramas that these essays try to sustain,’ he writes, ‘is the antagonism between the already narrated, examined life of developmental theory and the always potential life implied by the idea of the unconscious.’ Stating his own preference for psychoanalytic writing that aims to ‘evoke by provocation’ and then demonstrating it in these pithy, often ironic essays, he also acknowledges the necessary counterbalancing existence of a more instructive and knowing kind of psychoanalytic writing. Throughout the book he plays off one idea against another in this way - not usually in order to choose one and reject the other, nor to resolve the differences between them, but rather to see what might show up when two beams of light are directed to the experience in question from almost opposite directions.

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache

London

Robert Tollemache  

Here are two very different books on narcissism. Symington's is in lecture format and style and grandiose in proposing a new theory of narcissism. Mollon's is academic, precise, classificatory, based on other writers' work. Is it a surprise that they scarcely cover any of the same ground?

Symington reports in the preface that the book is the result of simply transcribing ten lectures on narcissism which he gave in Sydney, with the aim of preserving the lecturer-to-audience style. For me, this gain is outweighed by the loss in discipline and structure that it could have had, had he re-written it as a book. Although each chapter is said to address a separate topic, he often seems to be covering similar ground with only minor developments in argument. The obvious parallel is with his other book based on a lecture series, The Analytic Experience. There the lecture transcript model worked much more effectively; maybe this was because each lecture/chapter was so distinct, unlike this book, but also I suspect he put more work into transforming the lectures into separate chapters. With this book, he tells us he did not have time to edit his lecture transcripts into book form and had to leave it to someone else. I think it shows.

The central theme of the book is ‘the Lifegiver’ - a mental object that the mind can ‘opt for or refuse at a very deep level’. This is an emotional object associated with the breast or the mother, or in later life with another person, that a person seeks as an alternative to seeking oneself. If a person is to be ‘a source of creative emotional action’, there has to be a turning to and a taking in of this life-giving object; the turning away from the Lifegiver is the core of narcissism. Drawing on Fairbairn, he says that the Lifegiver cannot be wholly repudiated so the self is split, and one part turns against the Lifegiver.

Symington outlines a number of potential consequences from this turning away from the Lifegiver. The person can eroticise himself, by enticing others to be his source of action, since he cannot be the source of his own action due to his internal split. Or, by becoming the admired figure, he avoids envy; but this causes a vacuum at the centre, therefore he needs repeated stroking or stimulation, through drugs, sexual affairs, or the avoidance of disagreeable reality. Turning away from the Lifegiver also includes cruelty to others or self; avoiding self knowledge; projecting need onto others and then caring for them; and retaliating when hurt, not reflecting. For me, much of this goes beyond what we ordinarily call narcissism and seems tantamount to saying, ‘everything is narcissism’.

Tirril Harris

Tirril Harris

11 Bedford Square, London WCIB 3RA

Tirril Harris  

This is a surprising contribution on many levels. For many of us the surprise involves its seeming departure at right angles from the corpus of Langs' work, so well summarised in his recent clinical workbook (Langs 1992a). But in this paper his welcome earlier suggestions about genuinely communicative psychotherapeutic interventions are so encrusted with the clay of metaphor from the physical sciences that it is like archaeology to find anything to link it with his previous work. Devoted readers of this Journal, however, may find this article less unexpected: they will be aware from a book review last autumn (Livingstone-Smith 1993) of the simultaneous publication of two very different volumes which are not easy to synthesise (Langs 1992a, 1992b). And they may remember a paper some five years ago where Langs advocated the introduction of mathematics into psychoanalysis in order to permit ‘dynamical system modelling’ to impart ‘fresh views of psychoanalytic interaction and the process of cure’ (pp. 209, 210, Langs 1988). On the other hand, while the memory of this 1988 paper may have prepared some readers for Langs' enthusiasm for scientific research in psychoanalysis, they may still be taken aback by the absence in the current contribution of many of the concepts, theories and authors, largely deriving from chaos theory, which were cited there. This is a totally new language with a mass of very recent citations.

In itself novelty is far from being a problem but, in the case of trying to communicate so much that is new all at once within the 30-page limit imposed on journal articles, the authors have taken on a difficult task. Knowing their banquet could never fit into such a tiny vessel, they have opted to give us only the menu headlines rather than serving any of the courses. As a result the reader is left feeling unfed or, the intellectual equivalent, unconvinced. Perhaps they saw this as the most likely way to stimulate our appetites and motivate us to search elsewhere via the references for more specific examples of the chefs' actual creations. It would be unfair in this case to concentrate on this paper alone, given the inevitable shortcomings entailed by such restricted space for exposition.

This paper traces the psychological implications of Sophocles' treatment of the Oedipus legend, in the light of Bion's concept of ‘catastrophic change’ and Keats's of ‘negative capability’. Bernard Burgoyne

Bernard Burgoyne

Queensway, Enfield, Middlesex EN3 4SF

Bernard Burgoyne  

The first thing to say about this work is that it contains a remarkable achievement. The authors identify and construct variables with which to formalise aspects of communication between patient and therapist, and do so within structures commonly used in physics. In addition to this, their results have a virtue that is both striking and important: they allow for some fairly simple formulations to be made of the dynamics of the systems they are describing. Thus this work is powerful and, even though difficult, accessible. The second thing to say about their work is that it has left behind Freud's classical formulations of psychoanalysis, and with that has abandoned the psychoanalytical theory of the unconscious.

At one level, at least one of the authors seems aware of this: ‘the communicative approach is very much an outgrowth of psychoanalysis’ and, in terms of one of the variables that he uses for his communication theory, ‘it emerged that selective unconscious perception was far more pervasive than unconscious fantasy and distortion (transference)’ (Langs 1989). However, the term ‘psychoanalysis’ appears in the title of this paper, and ‘psychoanalysis’ and ‘the unconscious’ regularly appear in the development of the text, so there is a problem to address.

From the beginning of Freud's work, a central place was given to functions of distortative transformation. There are in particular two main operations involving the notion of distortion endemic to consciousness that are already present in Freud's work by 1900. The first is the compulsion to construct fictive accounts of reality, experienced by consciousness as a result of the inability of the ego to tolerate gaps in consciousness brought about by repression (Freud 1895):

There seems to be a necessity for bringing psychical phenomena into causal connection with other conscious material. In cases in which the true causation evades conscious perception one does not hesitate to attempt to make another connection … although it is false.

Further to A Question of Ownership: Response to ‘Who Owns Psychoanalysis?’, A Letter from Jeremy Holmes

Jane Kitto

Jane Kitto

2 The Park, London N6 4EU

Jane Kitto  

This short paper was prompted by the Letter from America by Jeremy Holmes (1994) in this Journal entitled ‘Who Owns Psychoanalysis?’ His title struck me as apt indeed for I believe the question of ownership lies at the heart of the problems faced by the analytic institutions in this country. I have discussed some of the consequences that I believe flow from this problem of ownership elsewhere (Kitto 1988). It is interesting that it is not the academic aspects of psychoanalysis that present a problem of ownership. Quite the reverse, these are, and have been since the beginning, firmly in the public arena, the province of philosophers, psychologists, anthropologists and others, not to mention the recent university departments. The ownership problem is about the clinical and professional aspect where status, employment and referrals are at stake. Dr Holmes's example from the United States is instructive, indeed the problems he lists can be seen here as has often been pointed out, for example, infantilising, pathologising and the failure to relate psychoanalytic work adequately to the wider context.

In October 1993 I gave a brief paper to the members of the London Centre for Psychotherapy at a day conference on the subject of organisational identity. These two questions of ownership and identity are so closely entwined that perhaps it is not surprising that many of Jeremy Holmes's ideas coincide with mine. It is always a comfort to discover that someone is in agreement with you, particularly on a subject as controversial and heavy with history and tradition as psychoanalysis and its institutional arrangements, and so I approached the editor who kindly agreed to publish what is a shortened version of the paper on identity I gave last October.

There is a problem of identity which all the organisations practising what is called analytic psychotherapy face in one way or another, arising from the question: what is analytical psychotherapy and how is it different from psychoanalysis?

Psychoanalysis and Cognitive Analytic Therapy

Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

London SE1

Anthony Ryle  

I am very grateful to the Editor for publishing, alongside my paper ‘Addiction to the death instinct?’, the commentary by Ann Scott, and grateful to her for the tone and contents of her remarks. The opportunity to respond in turn to the points she raises gives me the chance to spell out more positively the agreements and disagreements between CAT and Psychoanalysis.

Practical Issues

It is clear that CAT can treat many more patients per therapist or per budget than can either psychoanalytic psychotherapy or psychoanalysis. But this would be of no interest if it were shown to have no lasting, humanly valuable effects. We have accumulated enough experience to know that this is not the case, even with patients with border-line and narcissistic personality disorders of the type discussed in Joseph's paper. Most of what I say here will refer to this group. Who can benefit in what ways can only be clarified by careful research and we are currently accumulating a series of such patients treated with 16-24 sessions and to be followed up for as long as possible. The therapies are being audiotaped with the aim of documenting the process and relating it to outcome. It would be excellent if a group of psychoanalytic therapists would undertake a parallel study.

Theoretical Issues

To move on to theory, yes, it is my belief that ‘damage comes primarily “from outside”’ or, more precisely, from the interpersonal field in which the individual is formed. This does not deny that we are born with different potentials for love and hate and different thresholds to harm. But having assessed around 200 borderline patients in the course of my life I am angered by the scant attention paid to actual life experience in the accounts of most psychoanalytic authors. In the face of the abuse, torture and neglect suffered and, in most cases, at least partly remembered by these patients, it is insulting and misleading to explain their destructiveness and damage in terms of ‘ego weakness’ or a large dose of the death instinct.

[[RunningHead]]

Problems of Identity in Multi-Disciplinary Teams: The Self and Systems in Change

Anne Scott

Anne Scott

Lansdowne Clinic, 3 Whittingehame Gardens, Glasgow G12 OAA

Anne Scott  

Rapid changes in the ethos and functioning of the NHS are examined in the light of their effect on the multidisciplinary team members of a psychotherapy service. A process account is given of the nature of the changes in the service, the early emergence of difficulties in the team and their identification in psychodynamic terms. Some preliminary solutions are discussed. A theoretical discussion examines the need for an alternative meta psychology, involving the concept of the autonomous self and open systems theory, to aid our understanding of the process by which a system change can provoke psychic disturbance in the individual.

Competencies

Chris Whyte

Chris Whyte

Chris Whyte  

The Employment Department has established a number of Lead Bodies under the National Standards Programme. Each Lead Body is responsible for setting the standards required for National Vocational Qualifications (NVQs) for the various occupations within its remit. The methodology (functional analysis) is not negotiable, having been agreed by the Employment Department and the National Council for Vocational Qualifications. Essentially this means that Lead Bodies will define the competencies required for the NVQs in their field of employment.

The Lead Body for Advice Guidance and Counselling was established in 1992 and has already drafted a list of the competencies for these occupations. The United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy (UKCP) at its annual general meeting in January 1994 decided to ask this Lead Body to consider the feasibility of including psychotherapy within its remit. This decision was taken in the belief that NVQs are likely to be the qualifications of the future and on the grounds that psychotherapy seems to belong in the same family as advice, guidance and counselling. The UKCP has thus agreed to participate in a process that aims to define the competencies deployed in psychotherapy. This article was prompted by that decision.

[[RunningHead]]

Chair's Remarks: Conference, January 1994

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith

Regent's Park, London NW1 4NS

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith  

This has been a momentous year for the profession of psychotherapy. The United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy was established on 10 January 1993 and our national voluntary Register of psychotherapists was launched at the Houses of Parliament on 20 May 1993. These historic events have defined psychotherapy as an autonomous occupation in the United Kingdom. UKCP provides a matrix for a pluralistic profession, accommodating and respecting differences of method and philosophy, whilst maintaining firm boundaries and high standards for the training and practice of psychotherapists. It is from the robust safety of this matrix that we are now able to confront the important external challenges that face us.

The past twelve months have shown the importance of continuing to ensure that we can procure a safe and trusting environment, where there is room for internal debate and questioning in the spirit of cooperation and mutual respect. In order to safeguard this we need to maintain an open flow of communication as well as setting clear directions for decision making and executive action. The Governing Board is proposing to make some adjustments to our structures so as to achieve a better balance between the need for independent operation of individual units and effective feed-back and consultation throughout the organisation. This is a matter of fine tuning rather than a major reorganisation. We must be prepared to continue improving our organisation as and when this seems appropriate.

As UKCP has grown from a small voluntary organisation into a significant professional body, distinctions have to be made between different levels of decisionmaking and each has to be situated appropriately. The Governing Board has streamlined its modus operandi and needs to confirm this with some amendments to the constitution. These will link all major committees to the centre, making all chairs of committees and boards into officers and ensuring that the executive group is therefore truly representative, taking its brief from the Governing Board and reporting to it.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

As I take up the position of new Editor with this issue, it is timely to reflect on the immense contribution made by Bob Hinshelwood in founding the Journal ten years ago, and nurturing it over the years into its present robust state. It has become, under his sustained effort and creative guidance, a leading publication in the field of psychotherapy. For its continued vitality and future growth, we rely on the readers and authors, hopefully many new ones, whom we encourage to send articles, personal viewpoints and letters.

I have found the Editorial Board and the Editorial Advisory Panel to be impressively well-functioning in assessing the papers submitted for publication. We welcome several new members to the Editorial Advisory Panel with this issue, and warmly thank the present members serving on the Board and the Panel who give generously of their time and expertise to the work of assessment. The Journal is also fortunate to have the talents of Ann Scott, a most capable Deputy Editor, who will continue to organise the Annual Lecture and Student Essay Competition. Our Eighth Annual Lecture, this October, features two speakers, Professor Peter Fonagy and Dr Anthony Ryle, who will jointly address ‘Psychoanalysis, cognitive-analytic therapy, mind and self. We expect this to be an exciting and innovative event. Paul Gordon has had to step down as Book Reviews Editor after an excellent period in office, for which we are most grateful; we are delighted to welcome Melanie Hart from the Lincoln Centre who takes up the post with this issue. We are also fortunate that Marie Bridge will continue to edit the Clinical Commentary section. This issue contains a stimulating Commentary section, and whether one agrees or not with the presentation, one's own ideas are crystallised in a feeling of recognition and participation in the therapeutic dialogue.

The Journal will proceed in publishing a wide range of theoretical, technical and clinical articles within the various frames of reference for psychoanalysis and its applications. It is an exciting era for psychoanalytic psychotherapy as it takes up the challenge of developing and integrating new ideas from infant research, controversial but important studies of recovered memories of sexual abuse, and studies of borderline and narcissistic disorder. These areas will be addressed in future issues of the Journal. Our practice, inconceivable without its firm footing in the traditional theories, is yet inevitably informed and influenced by the array of new technical developments, theoretical models and striking case studies that form the core of psychoanalytic discourse. As we think about our work within, around and through our theories, it is by the effort of putting our (sometimes fleeting) thoughts into words that we discover the new, preserve the valuable, relinquish the mistaken, and make headway towards the increased effectiveness of our therapies. In the iconoclastic mood of the moment in the wider culture, one of dismissal not discernment, Freud has been accused of ruthless ideological imperialism and wilful falsification of clinical data. To practitioners of analytic therapy, this era of ‘Freud-bashing’ appears anomalous 100 years after Freud, imbued and trained as we now are in an anti-speculative attitude and a scrupulous wariness about imposing our beliefs on patients.

Roger Bacon  

This paper starts by suggesting that ‘talking’ in the ‘talking cure’ is a relatively unexamined phenomenon in psychoanalysis. It then proposes a re-assessment of talking as an achievement from the interactional perspective of Jerome Bruner and his colleagues. This in turn, it is suggested, has interesting implications both for the notion of ‘cure’, and for the place and function of the analyst in the dynamics of the treatment.

The Value of Psychotherapy

Francesca Denman

Francesca Denman

Francesca Denman  

Current research into Psychotherapy outcomes is reviewed in so far as it bears on the information needed to evaluate the value of purchasing psychotherapy services. Three aspects of psychotherapeutic treatment are discussed separately: efficacy (does it work), efficiency (how well does it work) and acceptability (how ‘nice’ or ‘nasty’ is it to take). It is argued that the existing research supports a cautious but positive assessment on all these aspects.
