Internship: Fact or Phantasy?

Samuel Stein

Samuel Stein

7 Sadler Walk, St Ebbes, Oxford OX1 1TX

Samuel Stein  

Many doctors have experienced their internship as a traumatic initiation into the medical profession. Rarely questioned, the process has resulted in a traditional cycle of distressed and unhappy interns. This article is an attempt to understand and clarify the institutional dynamics which are responsible for creating and maintaining these adverse patterns of behaviour. It concentrates on the interaction between the intern's inner phantasy world, the impact of the external hospital situation and the social defences which the hospital develops to protect its staff against the pain and anxiety inherent in their work. These collective social defence mechanisms often fail to protect the intern from intense anxiety and instead contribute to the hospital's increasing rigidity and resistance to change.

[[RunningHead]]

Wild Desires and Mistaken Identities: lesbianism and psychoanalysis by Noreen O'Connor and Joanna Ryan. Published by Virago, London, 1993; 315 pages; £12.99 paperback.

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Canterbury

Janet Sayers  

Homosexuality throws into question a fundamental tenet of psychoanalysis - its implication that one cannot desire the sex with whom one identifies. This impossibility, according to psychotherapists Noreen O'Connor and Joanna Ryan, is entailed by the theory that Oedipal desire for one parent involves identification with the other. Psychoanalysis accordingly deems lesbian desire only possible provided the lesbian identifies as a man. Or, if she identifies as a woman, it characterises her desire as pre-Oedipal, pre-genital, and as therefore not really sexual. Either way it reckons lesbian identity or desire spurious and hence necessarily pathological.

O'Connor and Ryan proceed systematically to demonstrate the operation of this maxim in a variety of psychoanalytic texts, beginning with Freud's and Helene Deutsch's lesbian case histories. They at least acknowledged some diversity in lesbian desire. Not so Karen Horney, Ernest Jones, Melanie Klein, Hanna Segal and other post-Freudians. These analysts variously characterise it as defence against desire for the father, or as pre-Oedipal regression, understood by some as involving refusal to know about, or envious attack on, the parental couple and their creativity.

This implies that lesbianism involves borderline psychosis. But, write O'Connor and Ryan citing examples from their own practice, this is by no means an inevitable feature of lesbianism. They likewise provide clinical vignettes to dispute Joyce McDougall's characterisation of the lesbian as identified with her father.

Integrity in Depth by John Beebe. Published by Texas A&M University Press, College Station, USA, 1992; 165 pages; $19.30.

Jean Thomson

Jean Thomson

London

Jean Thomson  

Does the psychotherapy movement represent a search for health or the provision of treatment for illness? In the earlier days of the NHS this was not an either/or choice but a spectrum covering prevention of disease, enhancement of living, hospital treatment as part of a dynamic community mental health service. These reflections came into my mind as I read John Beebe's book. Hopes of wholeness and integration underlie the philosophy of unified health provisions but his book reminded me that psychoanalytically-based therapies are still struggling for a permanent place. The Jungian approach to psychotherapy involves the view that the perception of opposites lies in every part of human experience so health and illness, therefore, as apparent opposites, can make sense in relation to one another when they are comprehended as parts of whole systems. Lacunae, traumas, misconnections, all have a role in achieving integration which John Beebe discusses as an inbuilt moral tendency. But it seems to require basic trust, and the loss or lack of this constitutes the dis-ease so that, in practice, the ‘talking cure’, in spelling out the nature of social and personal relations, stirs fears of catastrophe as much as it fosters hope.

Applying this to the social context, certainly in contemporary Britain, understanding the human capacity to make emotional links seems to have become anathema. Attention to a part causing problems, especially if given an apparent scientific validity by being statistically numerous, is sufficient remedy if as a result the whole system doesn't collapse. If the child fails, sack the teacher, don't query the context. After all, in a technological system like a motor car, if a sparking plug fails, all you need do is get another, so why should a system of humans be all that different? The psychotherapist who sees her work as part of the patient's inner search for wholeness, individual of social, with the idea that this equates with health comes to be seen as being on an esoteric quest. It seems to have been conceded that the materially rich, who are anyway indolent rather than ill and are used to chattering, have time to lie around five times a week on a couch. Only such have time to go over the experiences of earliest or latest life to try to see if the resultant shake-up in the kaleidoscopic interior system will result in an improved working of the body/mind/feeling constellation. In the eyes of the public in general, psychotherapy has been accepted if it does not take much time and can be used where crises and difficulties can be quickly sorted out. Discerning meaning or process, or the relation or one system to another, does not seem to have as much priority as finding the bad effect and arranging its elimination. Or so it sometimes seems when hearing the fragmented nature of ‘news’ and public information and the constant iteration that ‘costs’ always mean money. Yet, into this time where there is ‘no time’ for psychoanalytic ideas, more and more trainings are providing for more and more distressed people seeking counselling and psychotherapy help. John Beebe's book opens up the almost infinitely wide discussion of the integrity of our work.

From Fetus to Child: an observational and psychoanalytical study by Allesandra Piontelli. Published by Routledge, London, 1992; £40 (hardback), £ 14.99 (paperback).

Joan Raphael-Leff

Joan Raphael-Leff

London

Joan Raphael-Leff  

The field of fetal research is a rapidly expanding one, constantly producing extraordinary findings on fetal sensory capacities and behavioural states. Even in the last few months axioms about the pregnant ‘unit’ have been challenged as evolutionary biologists declare that the genetic interests of fetus and expectant mother are not always identical and, indeed, at times are antithetical since only half the baby's genes come from the woman's ovum. It is now well established that far from being the passive creature once imagined, the fetus not only responds but initiates: changing position to increase comfort; affecting the interuterine environment; altering maternal biochemistry to accommodate his or her needs and, seemingly, even determining the duration of gestation by provoking labour.

Since its publication, From Fetus to Child has won considerable praise for its groundbreaking behavioural observation of fetuses. It has also provoked some criticism regarding its methodology and the validity of its conclusions regarding prenatal ‘memories’ and continuity between behaviour patterns observed in the womb and after birth. To my mind, the book's undoubted value for those in the therapeutic professions lies in its descriptive base. By presenting sections of unedited (albeit selected) material from pre- and postnatal observations and analytic sessions with six very young children, Dr Piontelli offers us opportunities to draw our own conclusions -disturbing our complacency while providing us with rich food for thought. Readers of this book will find it difficult to adhere to a stereotyped view of a blissful intrauterine paradise of fetal oblivion; or indeed, an unquestioned idea of perinatal ‘fusion’ and neonatal undifferentiated nonentity.

Father Hunger: fathers, daughters and food by Margo Maine. Published by Gurze Books, Carlsbad, CA, 1991; 254 pages; £7.99.

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Canterbury

Janet Sayers  

Here's a book with a difference. For years therapists have focused on the material causes of women's eating disorders. Now, in Father Hunger, clinical psychologist Margo Maine tells us of their paternal origin. Not that this has always been overlooked. Freudians initially attributed anorexia to pubertally-revived Oedipal desire for the father against which the anorexic defends by regressing to infantile orality. Subsequently, still attending to orality, analysts have attributed eating disorders to infancy itself, to difficulties in the pre-Oedipal baby's relation with her mother.

Some argue, in Kleinian terms, that anorexia stems from early death-instinct based hatred of the mother resulting in the fantasy of orally incorporating her as a persecuting object within the self; this is exacerbated by puberty which renders girls bodily more similar to the mother against which they may rage by anorexically or bulimically attacking themselves. Others, following Fairbairn, attribute eating disorders to the mother depriving and not meeting her daughter's needs in infancy, against which she defends by internalising her as an exciting and frustrating object to be controlled from within, and against which she may then storm in adolescence as though this maternal object were the same as her body.

Fairbairnians, Kleinians and other object relations analysts disagree whether the baby's instincts or the mother's behaviour are more to blame. They agree, however, that the effect is a fantasy, namely that of orally incorporating the mother. By contrast many US and feminist therapists, influenced by Talcott Parsons' sociological reformulation of psychoanalysis, neglect fantasy in favour of focusing on sex roles instead. Boys, they argue, learn early to become individuated and emotionally distant from others thereby acquiring the instrumentality required of them at work. Girls, on the other hand, retain from early mothering the emotional connection with others necessary to becoming mothers themselves. In thus learning to attend to others' needs, however, they become alienated from their own. Hence the self denial of anorexia and the indiscriminate bingeing of bulima.

A View from the Battlefield

Chris Corcos

Chris Corcos

Chris Corcos  

What strikes me most about Sam Timimi's paper is the sense of fragility, helplessness, vulnerability and doubt that haunts the neophyte group therapist working in a psychoanalytic setting like the Cassel. Soon after taking up the post here, I too experienced desperate cravings for skill, a sense of mastery and with it a reasonably secure conviction that I was doing good rather than harm - or nothing. All the anxieties that Sam Timimi likens to those experienced by the student teacher crowded in early. I have been particularly prone to that fantasy that if I ‘did this or that’, which a more experienced therapist would surely know immediately to do, then important and live issues would spontaneously emerge, be examined, then worked through by the group and healing would take place. But my neurotic craving for ‘how to do it’ instruction has been systematically frustrated - even from before I took up the position of registrar here. Attending the hospital for a pre job meeting with the consultant and senior nurse on whose team I would be working, I asked for suggestions for useful reading, taking out my notebook and pen in eager anticipation. No such suggestions were forthcoming. Neither was my embarking on a personal analytic psychotherapy mandatory though its value for a therapist new to the analytic approach was acknowledged.

This culture of deferring gratification, tolerating the anxiety rather than feeling compelled to seek immediate relief from it, allowing oneself to discover one's own resources for containment rather than having to be contained by another (supervisor, therapist, published authority), this is the sea that we all swim in here. As intended, this philosophy has come to shape my work with my patients just as it shapes my supervisor's work with me.

Some months before I started at the Cassel a consultant psychotherapist who had recently joined the staff at my previous hospital, and who had worked at the Cassel years before in the very post that Sam Timimi and I now write about, put an avuncular hand on my shoulder, looked at me with a mixture (so I thought) of amused pity, hopelessness and deep sympathy. He said ‘You're going to feel very de-skilled for the first six months’. I write this with that first six months behind me, about to embark on the last three, and full of relief and anticipation that when I go into work tomorrow I will not feel de-skilled any more.

The Gender Conundrum: Contemporary Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Femininity and Masculinity by Dana Breen. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 1993; 304 pages; £40.00 (hardback); £16.99 (paperback).

Barbara Lloyd

Barbara Lloyd

Sussex

Barbara Lloyd  

This volume provides the reader with an opportunity to ponder upon and bring up to date their understanding of one of the central issues in psycho-analytic theory, sexuality. Its editor, Dana Breen, has drawn together writings from three cultural traditions - American, British and French and provided a thoughtful framework. The fourteen papers which are reprinted here first appeared between 1968 and 1990; only four were published before 1984. They are grouped in four sections: the Oedipus complex, the phallic question, the representation of the body, and bisexuality. In addition to a 39-page general introduction, Breen contributes a preface to each section; the first two are extensive.

The gender conundrum of the title is the tension which exists within the corpus of psycho-analytic theory between a focus upon biological destiny and a concentration upon the psychological construction of sexuality over time. Drawing upon Freud's struggle to describe masculinity and femininity and his concept of bisexuality, Breen identifies the essential body/mind duality in classical theory. Members of each sex group struggle to understand the specific significance of their anatomy in their lives. The theoretical task of comprehending this development is made more complex by the inherent bisexuality of human nature, the shared experiences of the nursling, female and male, and the intellectual traditions within which psychoanalysts work.

In a brief review it may be more valuable to give an indication of the issues which Breen identifies rather than listing the names of contributors or proffering a highly condensed overview. The introduction furnishes the reader with a concise theoretical summary from the historical perceptive of all three cultural traditions, first of women's and then of men's psychosexual development. We are reminded that Freud's final attention to pre-oedipal attachment to the mother led him to view bisexuality as more important in female development. Young girls' early sexuality becomes problematic as a consequence of their initial homoerotic object choice. An overlap between a phallic biological sexuality and phallic psychosexuality in young boys is not challenged by their pre-oedipal object choice. The conflict between a receptive and phallic sexuality is highlighted for girls by attachment to their mothers.

The Quantum Self by Danah Zohar. Published by Flamingo, 1991; 245 pages.

David Mann

David Mann

London

David Mann  

This is a bold book attempting to relate the complexities of quantum physics to the development of the self. It is only within the last couple of decades that the ideas from

591

quantum mechanics have really begun to filter from the rarefied atmosphere of modern physics into other areas. This book is part of that process.

Zohar shows how Cartesian philosophy and Newtonian physics were dominating influences that have shaped modern culture's view of everything from science to the cult of the individual. She convincingly demonstrates how Newton's theories lead to a conception of the universe as a lifeless design and that this was ultimately the inspiration behind Freud's ‘dark psyche’. For 300 years physics has supported the mind/body split. Matter was conceived as mechanical with no sense of purpose of intentions. The spiritual and the psychological came to be seen as a separate side of life. I think Zohar over-states her case at this point: Newton was a devout believer in God and his ultimate explanation of why gravity did not cause all the planets to collapse onto each other was that he believed it was God who kept them apart. This, along with other odd ideas such as Newton's belief in the aphrodisiac qualities of unicorn horns, has been distilled out of his theories by later generations of physicists and philosophers. That said, the old Newtonian idea of dividing the world into space, time, matter and causality has a firm grip in the modern mind. Quantum mechanics claims, on the other hand, that not only is there no space separating objects, there are not even objects!

In quantum physics reality is indeterminate, just a matter of probabilities. This book assumes some knowledge of quantum mechanics and cannot be read as an introduction to modern science, though Zohar does take the reader briefly through key theories such as complementarity, Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principal, the many world theories, etc. Briefly stated, quantum mechanics describes the universe as one in which everything is linked at every point: the most distance point and the oldest event of the universe are related in an unbroken wholeness with the present world.

The Promise of Family Therapy

Sebastian Kraemer

Sebastian Kraemer

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Sebastian Kraemer  

The process of family therapy unleashes forces which are powerful, primitive and potentially theatrical. Family systems therapy has evolved with little acknowledgement, and even disparagement, of the influence of psychoanalysis. In doing so, it has had a revolutionary impact but also one which has diminished the role of experience, particularly in the therapist. There are signs of convergence between modern psychoanalysis and systems therapy, and both have refined techniques that foster the primary task of therapy, which is observation through participation. In order to achieve this, family therapists require their own special skills to protect them from being stage struck by the family/audience (who also provide the script). The positive connotation is just one of these techniques, and I try to unravel its workings from my own experience. Positive connotation is effective when it provokes a transformation in the therapist, which precedes any change in the family. It is a promising technique but it can lead one astray.

The Institutional Field: An Evolution of the Container Model

Antonello Correale

Antonello Correale

Via Cavalier D'Arpino, 26,00197 Roma

Antonello Correale  

In the case of severe pathologies, the function of the container in the psychotherapeutic setting becomes particularly important, but this function is made extremely difficult by the turbulence of the situation. In these cases, the container must provide three goals: a function of real limits, a means for the distribution and articulation of the projective identifications of the patient, a holding-elaboration of very intense emotional charges. In these particular cases, the function of the container becomes so complex as to necessitate an entire institution rather than a single therapist. The single therapist is not able to carry out his empathetic-interpretative function unless he is integrated into a larger group-institution.

In order to describe and interpret the modalities of the functioning of the container-institution, it is useful to adopt the model of the field which can be considered a refinement and evolution of the model of the container. An outline of the principal factors that constitute the institutional field is detailed as follows:

The field is derived from the array of shared projective identifications in a cammon pool and not only from an individual into another.

The field is a shared sensory area as defined by Bleger.

The field contains an array of suffuse, powerful emotions which charge the atmosphere of the institution.

The field is derived from certain originating-foundation fantasies.

The field is a derivation of the historical memory of each specific institutional group.

Clinical Klein by R D Hinshelwood. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1994; 260 pages; £16.95.

John Hill

John Hill

London

John Hill  

This is an immensely worthwhile book. Dr Hinshelwood warns us in his preface that psycho-analysts do not always write clearly and attractively. Indeed I have often reflected that one definition of a psycho-analyst might be a ‘novelist who can't write’. Dr Hinshelwood, however, can write and I found that what he has to say in this treatise was of particular personal interest in that he sets out and clarifies issues that were simply not addressed objectively during my own analytic training in the late 1950's.

At that time the analytic world was, in Britain at least, still dominated by echoes of the so-called controversial discussions of the early 1940's. The discussions were about interesting but containable divergencies of viewpoint about human development, while the controversy was about who was to be allowed to conceive and rear analytic children.

The importance of Dr Hinshelwood's book is that he takes a standpoint well beyond that somewhat sterile dichotomy and complements his excellent Dictionary of Kleinian Thought by focusing attention on the clinical evidence on which that thought is based and on the criteria of validation. He shows his usual mastery of a wide mass of material and, while describing the work of many analysts, brings to it his own distinctive imprint, so that even familiar ideas and events take on a fresh light as he writes about and juxtaposes them in his own way. His method is essentially chronological and he begins by asserting that: ‘Melanie Klein's contributions are so rooted in the basic Freudian discoveries that they cannot be comprehended without some understanding of Freud’. In particular he emphasises Freud's basic departure from hypnosis in seeking to give expression to what was not under control rather than attempt to control it by suggestion. This in turn leads naturally to the method of free association and to the investigation of childhood memories, dreams and the importance of symbol formation, noting importantly, as Dr Hinshelwood does, that symbols are essentially idiosyncratic to the individual and need careful observation and translation in each individual case.

John Clare

John Clare

London

John Clare  

This is a book about the analyst as deviant. Located at the outer limits of psychoanalysis, it is an account, by both patient and analyst, of a treatment in which a woman in a fragmented and violent delusional state tries to find her true self by cutting and bleeding using broken bottles and razors. Like a tale from the Twilight Zone the book is cloaked in the atmosphere of film noir: a clinical, impersonal office, a lonely analyst who is a stranger to New York, broken bottles in dark alleys, a woman who abandons the falseness of her perfect self in an addiction to cutting and blood. Written in a restrained tone Dr Nakhla's account comes to life only when he delineates the delicate issues of fear and hate in the countertransference. The parallel passages based on Grace Jackson's diary provide interesting echoes of her analyst's erstwhile countertransference hunches. She is ‘hacking away to find the self, talking is of no use and the analyst has to contain and restrain as she acts out her unintegrated state, often in his presence. The doctor is a cliff to which she clings, sometimes literally as he physically holds her, escorts her to the subway, takes her to a plastic surgeon and even visits her home to read her crucial diary. With the body as a transitional object for this self-mutilating patient, a sense of omnipotence emerges, incorporating the possibility of being rather than being done to. Through the separate/fused debris of regression she is able to move to a state of aliveness and the boundedness of a body self. This is the threshold of apperception, acknowledging the healthy private core of the self.

When I look I am seen, so I exist

I can now afford to look and see

I now look creatively and what I

apperceive I also perceive.

(Winnicott 1971)

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The central role of the unconscious, and the importance of exploring it so as not to be its servant, are notions fully embraced by analytical psychotherapists, and this issue features articles that explore the unconscious in various ways. As we know, Freud viewed the dynamic unconscious - characterised by repressed emotion, displacement, condensation, symbolism and timelessness - as more than pathology-based but necessary for a general psychology. So it is interesting to reflect that the new cognitive sciences offer models of the mind without a concept of the dynamic unconscious, and so a new version of the cult of the rational. The unconscious realm of primal phantasies and imagined scenarios is surely the dynamic energy source for creativity, and narrates relational force fields that can't be represented by information processing models. Enigmas in the consulting room are a matter of teasing out the disguised, split-off content and when we unearth unconscious ideas and patterns, whole areas of mind, behaviour and symptoms become comprehensible. Cultural and personal splitting, denial and repression will continue to be forces to reckon with.

Unconscious motives for wanting analysis are presented here in a new paper by Henri Rey which takes further his 1988 paper, ‘That which patients bring to analysis'. He elaborates how dying (or dead) inner objects are brought into analysis to be rescued and repaired, and differentiates between schizoid repair and depressive reparation. Meanwhile, the self psychologists, although they abandon classical theory and transform psychoanalysis into a theory of self disorder and development, would maintain the central role of the unconscious and see their work as revealing unconscious archaic narcissistic structures and undeveloped areas of the self. One of the ‘fathers’ of self psychology, Ernest Wolf, writes of the position of theory and practice since he and Kohut wrote, 15 years ago, their seminal survey on disorders of the self. Then again, reports of the extension of the frontiers of unconscious influence into prebirth experiences occur with regularity nowadays. Naomi Rucker writes of what appears in the consulting room as shadows of intra-uterine life as they play on present-day experiences.

This paper addresses the meaning of psychological life before birth to later psychological experience as represented within the analytic process. The position is taken that residues of intra-uterine existence inevitably colour the internalisation of post-uterine experience. Imprints of prenatal relational patterns are brought into postnatal life as themes around which subsequent representations and imagoes are constructed. Echoes of prenatal motifs can be heard in the associations and modes of relatedness that are illuminated in the process of adult psychoanalysis. The experimental and theoretical literatures relevant to this premise are reviewed and clinical illustrations are provided.

Pauline Dalal  

In this volume, the third in a series, Freud's classical 1915 paper, ‘Observations on Transference-Love’, is presented along with ten papers by psycho-analysts of differing orientations. Their brief was ‘to extract the essay's important and enduring contributions, to clarify ambiguities and to establish some line of continuity between the original paper and current issues and concerns and to express the reviewer's own views as if he or she were teaching the paper.’

The outcome makes for stimulating reading and provokes thinking over a wide range of issues as contributors take up their individual perspectives. In addition to the central thrust of the original paper - Freud advising male therapists on how to understand and handle the ‘elemental passionateness’ of certain female patients - the paper itself and the reviews of it here raise other issues that are fundamental to psycho-analytic theory and practice: the nature of reality in the consulting room, analytic ‘truth’, acting out, the meaning and role of abstinence, and the nature of love.

It is also a timely publication given that the whole field of psychotherapy has been much under attack in the media for abuses of power and integrity. Freud is addressing these issues from the therapist's viewpoint. Though clear about the therapist's responsibility, he underlines the ‘explosive’ power of aspects of the transference relationship and how overwhelming these may be when the therapist has insufficient knowledge and experience. Freud insists that it is not the person of the therapist but his role that excites transference love. Some of the contributors remind us of the likely historical context, the fact that Breuer, Ferenczi and Jung were each burned by powerful erotic transferences and failed to maintain an appropriate position, thus compromising the treatment and the analytic truth that was Freud's passion.

Helen Morgan

Helen Morgan

London

Helen Morgan  

Few can have missed the fact that the practice of analysis and analytic psychotherapy is currently under increasing public scrutiny. When the challenge comes from those outside the profession who confuse analysis with the proliferation of fringe therapies, who are not aware of the rigours of the training, who react from fear and defensiveness, it is experienced as a wearisome and irritating attack. Whilst the process of registration has required the profession internally to examine itself, this has focused primarily on matters of technique and training. But training for what? What is it that analysis is about? What are its aims? Is it effective? And by what criteria and methods can this be assessed? It is the nature of the beast that such questions are hard to answer, but this does not make them valueless. Indeed, it may be that it is in the tussle with such questions that the potential for exciting and creative development lies.

In this book Plaut faces these fundamental issues head on and aims ‘to add a dash of scientific rigour to the unbridled hermeneutics into which I see analysis drifting’ (p. 343). The result is a critical, sometimes uncomfortable book that confronts many of the assumptions of analysis as well as the investment we all have in our particular set of theories. He avoids a clear yes or no, true or false, of scientism and emphasises instead the concept of faith and its necessary corollary, doubt. Plaut is no dissenter. His own faith is evident yet he is trying to view the profession critically from within and use his doubts to define its limits and its strength. Alongside references to what he terms Bion's ‘desiderata’ (‘without memory or desire’) he explores the notion of change as an aim for analyst and patient and the analyst's belief that her or his theoretical approach will bring about that change. This is a faith that, unless conscious and tempered by doubt, can become blind. Yet even the more open-eyed faith of ‘non-controlling expectancy’ that he hopes for has its limits. His discussion of the unchanging (and unchangeable) parts of all patients reminded me of the other connotation of the term ‘resistance’, that requirement for survival when faced with any totalitarian regime.

A Formal Science for Psychoanalysis

Robert Langs MD and Anthony Badalamenti PHD

Anthony Badalamenti

133 West 72nd Street, Suite 304, New York, NY 10023

Anthony Badalamenti  

Three modes of science are defined for psychoanalysis - domain, statisticalprobabilistic and formal. The last form is on a par with physics and seeks deep laws of nature through the use of quantified time series data to which mathematical models are applied. The paper summarises a research programme designed to bring formal science to the field. The models used are drawn from physics and include the power spectral density function (a measure of cyclical power), force and work, entropy or informational complexity (determined in two distinctive ways), and temperature (a measure of communicative activity). The evidence for a communicative force field is presented. The results are used to define three apparently universal laws of nature pertaining to human communication, each adhered to in distinctive fashion (individuality constrained by lawfulness). The limitations and implications of these initial results are discussed.

The Psychotherapist's Erotic Subjectivity

David Mann

David Mann

Flat 6, 164 Lordship Road, London N16 5HB

David Mann  

The therapist's erotic desires towards the client is a much tabooed and little discussed subject within psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. It is suggested that this topic needs to be opened up for scientific exploration and discussion. This paper is an investigation into the nature of the therapist's erotic subjectivity. A review of the literature suggests how difficult it is for many analysts to deal with their erotic desires towards the client completely successfully. Some clinical examples are given to illustrate how the therapist's erotic desires may make a positive contribution to the analysis. It is suggested that erotic desires are inevitable and are part of a healthy Oedipal development. The child needs to internalise and identify with the opposite sex parent's ability to contain incestuous longings. Like the parent, the therapist can expect to have sexual feelings for his or her clients. It is further suggested that objective erotic desires can be as useful as any other feeling the therapist might experience so long as they are analysed and understood in the client's interest.

Lynnett Fraser

6 Hereford House, Links Road, London W3 OHX

Lynnett Fraser  

This paper examines some long-term residues of childhood sexual abuse, drawing on relevant literature and focusing on a case study of a female patient seen three times weekly over a period of two years. I have attempted to explore the particular syndrome that is characteristic of those who have been sexually violated in childhood, by adults who also assume a position of trust. The clinical work provided evidence of the link between early maternal deprivation and vulnerability to abuse and I have illustrated my observations by emphasising the emotional context in which the abuse occurred. Specific difficulties of working with this patient are considered, including problems arising in the transference and the compulsion to repeat the traumatic experience both within and outside the therapeutic situation.

Validation in the Clinical Theory of Psychoanalysis: a study in the philosophy of psychoanalysis by Adolf Grunbaum. Published by International Universities Press, Madison, Connecticut; 417 pages; £45.00.

David Smith

David Smith

London

David Smith  

Far too many psychotherapists are ignorant of Adolf Grunbaum's contributions to psychoanalytic thought. Grunbaum is a philosopher of science, initially a specialist in the philosophy of space and time, who has turned his attention to the subject of psychoanalysis. A series of papers on psychoanalysis culminated in the publication of The Foundations of Psychoanalysis: A Philosophical Critique in 1984. In Foundations, Grunbaum pulled together the various strands of his criticism of psychoanalysis in a philosophical tour de force.

Grunbaum believes that Freud was a brilliant although ultimately unsuccessful scientific methodologist with much more penetrating insight into the problems inherent in the validation of psychoanalytic theory than his psychoanalytic contemporaries and heirs. Grunbaum therefore draws extensively on Freud's own reflections on the scientific status of psychoanalysis.

Grunbaum demonstrated in Foundations that there is precious little reason to believe in psychoanalysis. His arguments are elegant, impeccably logical and informed by a profound knowledge of Freudian theory. Grunbaum's first psychoanalytic book should have resulted in a tearing of hair and a gnashing of teeth throughout the world of psychotherapy. If psychoanalytic theory has no sound basis - if it is little more than a particularly compelling story - psychoanalytic practitioners should be very worried about what they are doing in their consulting rooms. They should be very worried about the interpretations they are giving and the fees they are collecting. In fact, very few psychoanalytic writers have realised the importance of Grünbaum's critique and engaged seriously with his arguments (e.g. Eagle 1984, 1986; Edelson 1984, 1988; Smith 1991a, 1991b).

Psychotherapists professing a non-Freudian faith may be tempted to applaud at this point. They have in reality no such cause for schadenfreude. Grunbaum seizes on Freud as a sort of paradigm case. Freud had the guts and the brilliance to concern himself with fundamental methodological issues. Once we get past Freud, philosophical agonising about the basis of one's psycho-therapeutic belief-system gets rather thin on the ground. And yet, all of the points made by Grunbaum apply in spades to the other forms of insight-orientated psychotherapy.

An unexpected setback in my professional life caused me to consider how disability in therapists may be regarded, both by fellow-members of the psychotherapy profession and by our clients. Response to ‘Castration Desire’ by David Mann

Francis Grier

Francis Grier

65 Tynemouth Road, London N15 4AU

Francis Grier  

I much enjoyed and was fascinated to read David Mann's paper ‘Castration desire’ (Mann 1994). Recently, as I was reading Freud's ‘A seventeenth-century demonological neurosis’, I came across a reference to the same subject (Freud 1923). Freud, however, approaches it from a slightly different perspective, which I thought might be usefully set alongside Mann's, not because it contradicts anything he says but because it expands his suggestions and, as it were, fertilises them. (Although Freud's remarks on this subject pertain to the central figure of his study, Christoph Haizmann, he explicitly uses the insights he derived from the Schreber case to make his point.)

In his paper Mann emphasises that the desire for castration is primarily regressive, embodying not only the young boy's emphatic wish not to be different from his mother, but also his craving ultimately to return to the womb. Mann also says that he wishes to distinguish castration desire from vagina envy, but it is here that I think Freud has something useful to add which lies between (and beyond) these two categories of envy and desire. For when Mann articulates what he means by vagina envy he emphasises emotional components pertaining particularly to the mother, especially the son's desire to be able to bear a child just as she can, and thus to become like her. The desire to be like her could correctly be construed, I think, as evolving from the child's envy of his mother, but equally from his love for her. Feelings, of whatever quality, about the father are conspicuous by their absence. The desire evolves on the part of the child neither to be separated from his primary object nor to be unable to do anything that his mother can; and so a yearning arises to disavow any growing awareness of difference from her.

But what Freud underlines are emotional components related particularly to the father, i.e. elements of the inverted Oedipus complex, primarily the son's desire to be castrated in order to be able to be loved by the father and thus to be able to have a child by him.

Stephen Frosh provides readers with the opportunity to re-examine their understanding of gender issues in psychoanalytic theory. His starting point is his discomfort both with the categories of difference which classical theory offers and with the limits which his masculine status imposes. The knowledge that men are responsible for most child abuse weighs heavily on him.

The argument is presented in six chapters. Although the writings of Klein are considered, Lacanian formulations and their reworkings by women, particularly French psychoanalysts, are examined in detail and afforded importance. In the first chapter Frosh asserts that masculine attributes are given precedence over feminine characteristics in psychoanalysis. He offers as evidence its therapeutic aim of expressing feelings in words, the goal of replacing irrationality with reason, and the significance of the Symbolic which is connected to the centrality of paternal law-giving.

In the second chapter Frosh confronts the pairing of the Imaginary with the mother and the Symbolic with the father and with patriarchy. If rationality is masculine, then the unconscious and its potential for disruptive activity is connected to femininity, but a femininity which is shared by women and men. It is the Imaginary and the regressive wish to return to perfect harmony and complete understanding with the mother which is disrupted by the intrusion of language, the Symbolic. The Kleinian assumption that the countertransference allows access to the inner world of the other is challenged from a Lacanian perspective using the Imaginary/Symbolic distinction. For Lacan, projection operates in the register of the Imaginary while introjection requires a developed understanding of the other; but it is this very symbolisation which limits knowledge of the ‘Other’. In addition, there is a tendency to elide ‘woman’ with the category of the ‘Other’ which, given the patriarchal resonances of the Symbolic, tends to marginalise femininity. Despite these complexities, ambiguities and suspicions Frosh maintains that sexual differences remain central in mediating any understanding of the other's inner world. Nonetheless, in the very act of describing sexual division, the subject, speaker, reveals a position as male or female.

Joy Schaverien PHD

Joy Schaverien

1 The Square, South Luffenham, Oakham, Leics LE15 8NS

Joy Schaverien  

The premise of this paper is that, in the treatment of anorexia, art psychotherapy has a specific contribution to make. In the case of severe eating disorders the client's relationship to food may be understood to be a means of negotiating and mediating between the internal world and the external environment. It is proposed that pictures may also mediate between the inner and outer world of the client and so between the client and the therapist. As an object of transference itself the art object may temporarily, and unconsciously, become a substitute for the use of food. It may serve a positive function as a Transactional Object. This is distinguished from the ‘Transitional Object’ (Winnicott 1971) and the ‘Transformational Object’ (Bollas 1987). The view accords with those who consider that anorexia is a borderline disturbance. Thus the anorexic client is considered to be functioning at a pre-symbolic level; she is concretising her experience and acting out through the use of food. If this need for concrete expression can be converted from an obsession with food to a use of art materials there is a beginning of a movement towards symbolisation.

The Role of Ambivalence in the Development and Use of Reproductive Technology

Christina Wieland

Christina Wieland

50 Fernleigh Road, London N21 3AL

Christina Wieland  

What I would like to explore here is some possible unconscious and denied motives behind artificial reproduction as well as, more generally, the scientific manipulation of nature, of which it is only a small part. I say a small part and yet, more than any other project that involves the manipulation of nature, artificial reproduction has the feeling of ‘playing God’. Images such as Frankenstein's monster - the nineteenth century's version of the scientific creation of life - and the Brave New World's mass production of test tube babies haunt our imagination and remind us of the unconscious monstrous underside of science.

Hubris is the Greek word for humankind's omnipotent denial of its limitations - of its ‘playing God’. Hubris can be seen within the Oedipus complex as the rebellion against the father and the denial of his authority - ultimately the denial of castration. In this sense hubris would mean a theft and appropriation of that which does not belong to the son together with the grandiose phantasies of omnnipotence that such an appropriation creates. That was, I think, Mary Shelley's intention when she subtitled her book A modern Prometheus. In this Greek version Prometheus's theft remains the ambiguous and ambivalent foundation of science.

The theft from father is, however, secondary. Before that, and at a primary level, lies the theft from mother. To get to this primary theft we must look below the classical Oedipus complex into the early relation with mother. This early relation with mother involves an early identification with her for both boys and girls. Freud (1923) ignored this early identification with mother as far as the boy was concerned and stated instead in ‘the Ego and the Id’ that the boy's first identification was with his father. This is a different type of identification from the one he outlined in ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (Freud 1923):

This is apparently, not in the first instance the consequence or outcome of an object-cathexis; it is a direct and immediate identification with the father in his own personal prehistory.

Evelyn Adey

Cambridge

Evelyn Adey  

Delightful quotations from Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's Le Petit Prince head chapters throughout this book; they explain the title, encapsulate the psychoanalytic process and give a flavour of the liveliness of the book's content. To ‘tame’ is to differentiate and so to identify and know the uniqueness of the object, and thus, also of the subject. Only then is solitude meaningful. Liveliness may seem a strange word to use in the context of the deadening effects of separation anxiety, but Quinodoz's detailed and illuminating exploration of object loss leads to the feeling of buoyancy he describes in the last part of the book, so that reading the book offers a sort of experiential parallel to the process of working through separation anxiety.

In the first section of the book Quinodoz gives a general introduction to separation anxiety, provides a comprehensive clinical example and defines his terms. The word separation is used for the parting of whole object from whole subject and differentiation is used to describe the internal distiction between ego and object. Prior to differentiation, relating is maintained by means of projective identification and separation in this case leads to loss of parts of the ego and to fragmentation. Separation in a differentiated subject leads to normal mourning. Although theoretically differentiation precedes the ability to separate, Quinodoz points out that in clinical practice the processes are most often alternating or occurring simultaneously. In fact, throughout the book he is at pains to point out the importance of using theory to clarify thinking, while at the same time attending to the unique individual on the couch. Theory is, by definition, a generalisation from a multitude of clinical examples, and the generalisation has to be dismantled for each individual in the clinical setting. As Bion said, we strive to approach each patient without memory or desire.

The second section of the book concentrates on the different psychoanalytic theories of separation anxiety. This splendidly lucid account of the divergencies and congruencies in different theories is refreshing because it is rare for a single author to describe different theories with such sympathy and objectivity. Quinodoz himself is a Kleinian but clearly respects the other's right to find his or her own preferred way of conceptualising clinical material. Quinodoz's interest in exploring ways analysts of different orientations theorise about similar clinical matter almost amounts to a subplot running through the book. He points to differences which seem to be largely linguistic and others which seem incompatible.

A Personal Experience of Growth as a Therapist and Reflections on a Group Experience

Sami Timimi

Sami Timimi

127 Axminster Road, Holloway, London N7 6BT

Sami Timimi  

Introduction

I remember being a pupil in secondary school, in that crossing point between the continuing need for the security of the family and the desire for a more autonomous individual identity, at that age when personal growth demanded a more open challenge to parental authority. As symbols of parental authority, teachers were also on the receiving end of such defiance. Some, however, could contain pupils' behaviour better than others, and the class quickly and intuitively gained a sense of their capacity for this. Any hint of weakness was ruthlessly exposed and exploited.

This was particularly so with student teachers on placements. As soon as they were left to cope with the class on their own we would start all manner of testing to see how far the boundaries could be stretched. Tensions would rise and we would begin to see how well this new victim was going to cope with the ordeal - talking out of turn, making jokes, disobeying, complaining about their technique and so on. Their qualities of leadership and for containment of this adolescent, rebellious, antiauthority energy were under scrutiny, and in the weeks that followed both they and we would begin to discover what capacities they could find in themselves for this task.

I now have some idea of what these experiences may have been like for the student teacher. The feeling of being made to feel useless; the cruelty with which one feels one's inadequacies being exposed; the pressure and with it the wish that things could be different, that the pupils could be more reasonable, or that they could see your strength; the fantasy that if you did this or that, the pupils would miraculously respond to your abilities and a respectful working calm would descend.

Some of these feelings confronted me during the first few months of my nine-month placement as Registrar in Psychotherapy at the Cassel Hospital, seeing patients in combined individual and group therapy. It was a mode of therapy that was new to me. It now seems clear that no amount of preparation beforehand could have prepared me for the emotional demands that I was about to have to survive. At times it was ‘touch and go’ whether I could cope with this type of work, and it is only retrospectively that I can see more clearly the importance of actually experiencing the process in order to discover what internal capacities I possessed to deal with it.

Melissa Benn  

A little too much knowledge can be a dangerous thing. We live in a society characterised by growing technical information and awareness of the nature and quality of life before birth; as many a pregnant woman knows, the sheer number of tests and scans and ‘internal visions’ of her womb now available can paralyse and terrify her as well as provide her with much needed information. There is a parallel in our growing awareness of our internal psychic worlds. Pregnancy - the growth and sustenance of two lives beneath one skin - can bring with it a sense of awesome responsibility as well as primitive mystery. Emotions are inevitably turbulent: experienced, paradoxically, as both more raw, on the surface and yet more hidden, deep within us. How much can psychoanalysis help us with these other kinds of ‘internal vision’?

A great deal, according to this sane and helpful book. Drawing on many thousands of hours of interview with pregnant women, her own work as a psychoanalyst, and more academic work on the subject, Joan Raphael-Leff does the difficult thing of catering to two audiences: the pregnant woman with no particular psychoanalytic knowledge and the psychotherapist with no particular knowledge - perhaps - of pregnancy. Certainly, any reader who is or has been pregnant or might be contemplating pregnancy, or who has a partner in this position, will find this book very reassuring: in ‘snippets’ of talk through to fuller case histories, we are presented with the entire spectrum of emotion, joyful and anguished, relating to conception and childbearing. No pregnant woman could finish this book and think herself strange for whatever feelings pregnancy has evoked in her.

Dear Editor

The Association for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in the NHS is setting up a new section: Psychotherapy for Older Adults.

The section will foster professional relationships and the sharing of experience and ideas between psychoanalytic psychotherapists and others who work psychoanalytically with older people.

Psychoanalytic psychotherapy is increasingly valued in general as has been shown recently by the Royal College of Psychiatrists. There is also increasing interest in providing services for the elderly population. It is hoped that the establishment of the section will extend and combine these two areas of work.

The section will arrange open meetings with clinical and theoretical content and encourage and support informal links between health workers. It will also stimulate research and new ways of thinking in response to the demographic changes in the population and recent academic developments. The section hopes to arrange teaching seminars, supervision groups and the compilation of a bibliography.

The Celluloid Couch: Representations of Psychotherapy in Recent Cinema

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

16 Kenilworth Road, London NW6 7HJ

Paul Gordon  

To most people, I suspect, psychoanalysis in the cinema means Woody Allen, whether the many jokes about his own lengthy analysis or the depictions of psychoanalytic treatment in films such as Annie Hall (1977) and, more recently, Another Woman (1988) and Alice (1991). Yet the figure of the psychoanalyst or psychotherapist turns up in a surprising number of mainstream films, surprising given that psychotherapy remains very much a minority activity, whether one is speaking of practitioners or patients. Such figures may often be marginal but in several recent films (here I am talking of films mainly from the start of the 1980s) they, and the process of analysis or therapy, are central. But let me begin with a question. As someone who practises psychotherapy, have you ever done any of the following: eaten sweets from a jar while seeing a patient? shouted at a young patient whose brother had died in a tragic accident? thrown a book at a patient's relative? informed on a patient's political views to the plice? The questions are, of course, absurd but I ask them because psychotherapists have been shown as doing all these (and more) in several recent (and not so recent) mainstream films. Film psychotherapists, it seems, are by definition eccentric. This, it would appear, is a qualification for the job. Like the belted raincoat, cigarette and drink of the private detective of days gone by, the psychotherapist's hallmark is his or her varying degree of weirdness. In Duet for One (Andrei Konchalovsky 1986), Dr Louis Feldman (Max von Sydow) conducts psychoanalytic sessions from behind a desk while eating cough sweets from a large jar (even when he has no cough) and cuts articles from newspapers during a session. The caricature is matched in its risibility only by the portrayal in the same film by Julie Andrews and Rupert Everett of acclaimed concert violinists. (This film, with its parallels with the life of Jacqueline Du Pré, carries a particular resonance in that it is widely known that Du Pré did in fact seek analysis with a prominent psychoanalyst after she was known to have multiple sclerosis.) In Ordinary People (Robert Redford 1981) Dr Burger (Judd Hirsch) is loud and foul-mouthed (although in the end sympathetic); in Truly, Madly, Deeply (Anthony Minghella 1990) the (anonymous) therapist is mousy and unaccountably slow-witted; the therapist visited by disc jockey Dickie Bird (Bill Paterson) in Comfort and Joy (Bill Forsyth 1984) ends up more upset than the man who has come to consult him; and when weatherman, Phil Connors (Bill Murray) consults a psychologist in Groundhog Day (Harold Ramis 1993) the man is, inevitably, odd and clearly not up to the job.

Barbara Lloyd

Brighton

Barbara Lloyd  

In this book Doris Bernstein's innovatory approach to gender development is carefully gathered together and annotated by two of her colleagues at the Institute for Psychoanalytic Training and Research (IPTAR) in New York and made available to an interntional audience. In a career cut short by a debilitating illness and spanning only three decades, Bernstein was a pioneer, professionally as well as intellectually. Her life offers a model both of a professional woman, who combined a career with a family, and of a psychoanalytic clinician, who struggled against the medical monopoly of psychoanalysis in the United States. She negotiated IPTAR's accreditation by the International Psychoanalytic Association as the first American non-medical institute.

The prime focus of Bernstein's theory is a re-analysis of gender development in terms of the specific experiences of growing up in a female or a male body. Her account is firmly rooted in Freudian psychoanalysis and employs the concepts of the dynamic unconscious and of infantile sexuality; but where her gender specific approach differs from that of Freud is in the treatment of female sexuality. While accepting Freud's insistence on the significance of anatomical differences between male and female, Bernstein offers a positive account of the little girl's development. She furnishes an alternative to Freud's narrative of a secondary development, a shift in aim and object, made necessary by the recognition of lack. Her account challenges the orthodox view of a unisex development in which the phallic principle accounts for psychic structuration and sexuality, implying female weakness and a masculine form to genitality.

Speak Of Me As I Am: the life and work of Masud Khan by Judy Cooper. Published by Karnac Books, London 1993; 160 pages; £14.95.

Val Richards

Val Richards

London

Val Richards  

Two important contributions of Masud Khan to psychoanalytic theory and clinical practice were his concepts of cumulative trauma and the protective maternal shield, with the implication that psychological damage may occur less as a ‘once at a crash’, than as recurring psychic dents from which the mother has consistently failed to protect her child.

Judy Cooper's memoir of Khan's life and work is informed by the relationship of these concepts to Khan's own history and personality. A perpetual exile, even in Pakistan, the land of his birth, born of an aged, patrician father and a socially unacceptable courtesan, Khan saw himself as blending his mother's sensitivity with his father's autocracy. His lifelong unresolved turmoils seemed to embody the scandal of his conception from which maternal devotion could never adequately shield him. As a talented and well-favoured youth with the sole blemish of a deformed ear, he left Pakistan for London and the British Society, in an insatiable thirst for recognition, for renown - and for full analysis. Here, his intellectual virtuosity, diligence and clinical skills won him gradual, if reluctant acceptance. For his seemingly bottomless narcissism, with a grandiose disregard of established convention and clinical boundaries, sowed discord in his relationships, both professional and personal. The onset of cancer and its spread over the last twenty years of his life coincided with his increasing exclusion from the Society, which he bitterly ascribed to the disease rather than to his actual misdemeanours.

Shattered in adolescence by the deaths within a year of his father and beloved younger sister, Khan then had to face the loss, after a year in each case of both his analysts - Ella Sharpe and John Rickman. Finally, in Winnicott he found a holding and containing analytic mother/father who nevertheless - sadly for Khan - failed to withstand Khan's ‘destruction of the object’. Cooper quotes (p. 21 from Khan 1969, Vicissitudes of the Self, p. 75).

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 75, Part 1, 1994

The Analytical Third: Working with Intersubjective Clinical Facts

Thomas H Ogden

In this paper, two clinical sequences are presented in an effort to describe the methods by which the analyst attempts to recognise, understand and symbolise verbally for himself and the analysand the specific nature of the moment-to-moment interplay of the analyst's subjective experience, the subjective experience of the analysand and the intersubjectively-generated experience of the analytic pair (the experience of the analytic third). The first clinical discussion describes how the intersubjective experience created by the analytic pair becomes accessible to the analyst in part through the analyst's experience of ‘his own’ reveries, forms of mental activity that often appear to be nothing more than narcissistic self-absorption, distractedness, compulsive rumination, daydreaming and the like. A second clinical account focuses on an instance in which the analyst's somatic delusion, in conjunction with the analysand's sensory experiences and bodyrelated fantasies, served as a principal medium through which the analyst experienced and came to understand the meaning of the leading anxieties that were being (intersubjectively) generated.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 75, Part 1, 1994

The Invisible Woman

Rosemarie Krausz

This paper explores the meaning of experiences of invisibility in women. It was inspired in the course of psychotherapy with a woman who felt invisible in her feminine identity and who hid her feminine desire within an imaginary paper bag. Her visual imagery traces a pattern of pathological feminine development through a faulty sensory connection between her body, the external world, and her unconscious symbolic self-representation. Questions about her invisibility have evoked an exploration of two developmental models of visual thinking - a cognitive and a psychoanalytic model. A study of the myth of Persephone contributes a literary prototype for the understanding of the transmission of invisibility across the generations of mothers and daughters. Furthermore, the analysis of several literary passages from the work of Angela Carter serves the purpose of drawing the reader into the experimental world of femininity as it moves from the invisible to the visible. The paper blends together ideas from various, often contending, theorists in a way which highlights how theories can complement one another in explaining clinical phenomena.

Case examples are used to illustrate the human consequences of the significant levels of psychosocial morbidity in Britain today. A variety of psychotherapeutic interventions may reduce morbidity and also reduce the social costs such morbidity accounts for. The value of a psychotherapy assessment is emphasised as a way of matching resources and patients. In this connection the specialist role of the consultant psychotherapist is discussed.

For a skilful psychotherapist clinical hunches may be finely differentiated and reliable, yet the evidence on which they are based tends to remain pre-articulate. The prognostic significance of these considerations is discussed. The complexity of the issues and the value of thinking structurally are illustrated through a clinical study.

Psychic Work and Unconscious Alliances in Therapeutic Institutions**

René Kaes

René Kaes

32 Cours de la Liberté, 69003 Lyon, France

René Kaes  

In this paper I would like to take up the idea that there are institutional bases to the reality of the unconscious wish within the members of a team whose primary task is to care for subjects in distress. This leads me to wonder on what dimensions and functions of the institution the project of care is based and how the need for care is formulated in the institution. A specific place must be made amongst these dimensions for the unconscious alliances, pacts and contracts that are struck between the subjects - carers and cared for - in the institution.

These questions formulated from the clinical work of and on carers lead to the following: what is involved in providing care? Although it is hardly possible to answer it directly, my hypothesis is that the caring capacity is not the sole property of the individual subjects, but a property of the team formed by these subjects, in their intersubjective and institutional links; we are dealing therefore with an intermingling of links, with different logical levels, with separate psychic locations and places.

A second hypothesis is possible: not only are there, within the institution, elements that support the caring capacity of the team workers, but it may be these very elements that interfere with it. Our experience confronts us with the ambivalence involved in a founding activity, ambivalence which can be seen as one of the causes of the institutional reversal whereby an institution whose task is to provide care ends up operating a reversal of its aims and functioning so that it becomes a non-caring and even an anti-caring institution. This drifting away from and reversal of the primary task of the institution are not linked solely to the instinctual ambivalence located in the pair of opposites: caring-making ill. This dual move is inscribed within the organising phantasy which supports the unconscious positions of the subjects within an institution. Such a phantasy, or more often a phantasy configuration, constitutes the unconscious structure of the institution, defines the psychic relations of each to the common primary task (and the common unconscious purposive idea), regulates the fit between mental apparatus and subjectivity and constructs a psychic reality specific to the group and the institution (Kaës 1992).

The Clinical Implications of Attachment Theory

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes  

The work of John Bowlby, although influential in developmental psychology and social psychiatry, has had relatively little impact within his parent discipline of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The paper traces Bowlby's relationship with the British Psychoanalytic Society, contrasting his ideas with those of Klein. Drawing on recent findings in developmental psychology stimulated by Attachment Theory, it outlines the clinical relevance of the concepts of the secure base and narrative, and reviews notions of defence and the Oedipal situation from the attachment perspective. Attachment Theory is not a new ‘school’ of psychotherapy but addresses principles which underlie all effective therapies. An extended case study is described illustrating these points.

Working with a Twin: Implications for the Transference

Vivienne Lewin

Vivienne Lewin

24 Estelle Road, London NW3 2JY

Vivienne Lewin  

The relationship between twins is based on primitive mechanisms which need to be mitigated by a containing and processing mother for adequate emotional development to take place. Where this fails, the twins remain in an arrested state of development dependent on splitting and excessive projective identification, and unable to separate. This is reflected in the transference relationship, the psychotherapist being experienced as a twin, a reflection of the patient, rather than as a container. Through intervention in the twinship via interpretation of the transference relationship, the patient may be enabled to find the psychotherapist as a processing mother and to develop a sense of self, a separate identity.

J. Rey

J. Rey

L'eau coulee, Boute de la filatte, 17880 Les portes en re, France

J. Rey  

The concept of the internal objects and internal and external spaces has been further developed in this paper. These objects are an important part of patients seeking treatment for themselves for they are also looking unconsciously for ‘treatment’ of these objects. The objects are ‘damaged’ and the patient does not know how to repair them. He keeps them alive in the hope that help will come. The methods used to keep them alive, even when dying, have been described. The stages at which these objects have been, or are thought to have been, damaged is vital. For example, they can range from the sensori-motor level to higher levels of maturation, to produce psychosis, borderline or hypochondria. The concrete level is stressed for it leads to concrete repair as opposed to psychic reparation.

Be Reasonable

Jane Milton

Jane Milton

Jane Milton  

Dear Sir

Anthony Ryle (1993) has, I think, completely missed the point of Betty Joseph's paper ‘Addiction to near-death’ (1982). Following on from Ann Scott's critique (1993), with which I am in broad agreement, I would like to add a few thoughts of my own.

I am familiar with the work of both clinicians from the ‘inside’, so to speak, as they have both been inspiring and influential supervisors at different stages of my professional development. I think that if Ryle knew Joseph's work properly he is someone who would appreciate her incisive mind and her humane, light touch. The statement Ryle makes that Joseph's patient received ‘constant interpretation of gratification in destruction’ is a puzzling one, since it seems to me that the avoidance and analysis of such enactments is one of the very issues that she is addressing in the paper. In fact one of Joseph's major contributions to clinical psychoanalysis is her detailed attention to the fine grain of transference and countertransference patterns. A tendency to find oneself taking a moral stand with a patient who is submitting masochistically will be a total phenomenon to be observed and itself analysed, as it will give an important insight into the patient's inner world of object relationships.

It would be useful if all patients could be cured by reason. If they (and we, when we are patients!) could be shown rationally what they were doing with the help of diagrams even, and would say, after ten or fifteen sessions, ‘Oh yes, I see what I have been doing, I'll stop now, thank you very much’! This might work if human beings were a) basically well-meaning and nice all the time, really; b) could easily bear the sorts of psychic pain that their defences had so assiduously been developed to cover up; c) were never seriously perverse; d) all had readily available curiosity, concern emotional depth and capacity to mourn. In these circumstances cognitive understanding without major opportunity for working-through might be enough.

Hateful Relationships

Sue Gottlieb

Sue Gottlieb

Babbs Farm, Westhill Lane, Watchfield, Highbridge, Somerset TA9 4RF

Sue Gottlieb  

This paper explores some of the dynamics of hateful relationships between parts of the self as they are played out between patient and therapist. The patients described are dominated by a ruthless i nownternal object bent upon eliminating the most vulnerable parts of the self and the potentially helpful external object. In its most extreme form this type of hatred becomes psychotic when it destroys the means of perception. Also considered is the hatred experienced by the therapist, and a distinction made between ‘objective’ hatred and that resulting from the projection into the therapist of a hating internal object.

Varieties of Disorders of the Self

Ernest Wolf

Ernest Wolf

180 North Michigan Avenue, Chicago, IL 60601, USA

Ernest Wolf  

Fifteen years have passed since ‘The disorders of the self and their treatment: an outline’ (Kohut & Wolf 1978) presented an up-to-date survey of the progress that had been achieved in the development of self psychology. It seems now that the time is ripe for another stock-taking. Especially diagnosis, aetiology and treatment possibilities should be brought in line with accumulating clinical experience. The content and focus of this essay are determined by an attempt to clarify aspects of theory and practice that have remained problematical. Again, as in 1978, a classification of self disorders forms the centre of this survey.

Psychotherapy in the Third Age

Ann Orbach

Ann Orbach

19 New Park Road, Chichester, West Sussex P019 1XH, UK

Ann Orbach  

In this paper I discuss psychotherapy in old age in the context of our ageing society and ageist attitudes. I suggest that the therapist is as resistant as the ageing patient to themes of loss and death. I question the short-term therapy often recommended and use case material to show that, despite the strength of the transference and the difficulty of ending therapy, the older patient is as suitable for long-term psychotherapy as many of those in a younger age group whom we willingly agree to treat. In conclusion, I stress that the Third Age has been defined as a period for opportunity and new development.

Subjects of Analysis by Thomas Ogden. Published by Jason Aronson, Northvale, NJ, 1994; 230 pages; £16.95.

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Stevenage

Phil Mollon  

This is another fine work from the author of acclaimed earlier books such as Projective Identification and Psychotherapeutic Technique, The Matrix of the Mind and The Primitive Edge of Experience. Ogden has acquired a reputation for taking current concepts in theory and technique, explicating them with exceptional clarity and then creatively elaborating upon them. Although he is American and based in San Francisco, the psychoanalytic sources he draws upon are very largely British, especially in the Kleinian tradition; his period as an associate at the Tavistock Clinic was obviously very fruitful. The influence of Bion is clear. In previous books he has explored the concept of projective identification and has postulated a third psychic position, the autistic-contiguous, juxtaposed to the Kleinian paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions. In this book he ‘attempts in different -ways to explore a conception of psychoanalysis as a unique form of dialectical interplay of the individual subjectivities of analyst and analysand’. He writes of the ‘analytic third’, the unique events in the consulting room, to which both parties contribute, but which each experiences differently. In this respect, Ogden has much common ground with the ‘intersubjectivity’ emphasised by post-Kohutians such as Stolorow, even though the tradition they draw upon is profoundly different.

Ogden argues that whilst Freud presented the decentring of the subject from consciousness, it is not correct to state that the real subject is located in the unconscious - but rather in the dialectical interplay between consciousness and unconsciousness. He goes on to explore the dialectical dimensions of Klein's theories, the interplay between the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions, these being not linear stages of development but psychological organisations which each provide a context for the other, neither having meaning except in relation to the other. He also considers how the concept of projective identification describes the creation of the subject in the psychological space between infant and mother and analyst and analysand. He then explores dialectical aspects of Winnicott's accounts of the transitional space.

Universals of Psychoanalysis in the Treatment of Psychotic and Borderline States: factors of space-time and language by Henri Rey. Edited by Jeanne Magagna. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1994; 319 pages; £25.00.

Eric Rhode

Eric Rhode

London

Eric Rhode  

A cardinal in 1440 (Cusanus) wrote that the inhabitants of the moon lived in the betwixt and between and this is why they are lunatics. Anthropologists (notably van Gennep, Turnbull, Turner, Douglas) are fascinated by the betwixt and between as a function of closed societies: as the place, as well as a state of mind, where dwell marginals and social transitionals, either habitually (actors, transvestites, tramps) or temporarily, as initiates to cults or trainees, people who are changing professions or relationships, or involved in celebrations (like the carnival) or unusual processes like childbirth or dying, or passing through puberty and adolescence. In some cultures the betwixt and between is associated with illegitimacy, with states of being polluted or a pariah. It is above all associated with experiences of psychic death and possible rebirth, moments of paranoid-schizoid conversion or of depressive recognition.

A basic component in the psychoanalytic picture from the start has been the interim nature of human experience, lying, as it does, between primary and secondary process, conjecture in dream and waking thought. Freud's theory of the life and death instincts discovers a Shakespearean resonance in the interim.

In her remarkable 1935 paper, ‘A contribution to the psychogenesis of manicdepressive states’, Melanie Klein describes the meaning of the Freudian conflict in terms of the spatial concept of a threshold to the depressive position, a limen associated with death and suicide as well as development. Bion deepens understanding of the threshold in his theory of catastrophic change, which operates in analysis microcosmically as a function of any true interpretation, and macrocosmically as the turbulence intrinsic to major shifts in development. Bion's theory invites the clinician to focus on the transformatory impetus of states of psychic death in which conceptions of space and time become attenuated and former certitude disappears.

Henri Rey has an unusual contribution to make to this area of thought. He has a reputation as a clinician and teacher. Since his retirement from the Maudsley Hospital, he has spent time supervising groups and institutions around the world. Now Bob Young at Free Association books has brought together many of his papers and has elicited attentive editing from Jeanne Magagna and a useful introduction from John Steiner. Many of the papers are about Henri Rey's work in the short term as he has taken up temporary teaching posts about the world.
