The Psychoanalytic Mind from Freud to philosophy by Marcia Cavell. Published by Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA, 1993; 276 pages; £23.95.

David Smith

David Smith

London

David Smith  

Marcia Cavell, a psychoanalytically trained philosopher, has written this impressive book to show that certain strands of psychoanalytic theory can be underwritten by certain strands of contemporary analytic philosophy. Cavell is equally at home in the psychoanalytic and philosophical literature and moves with enviable ease from one to the other. Philosophically, she is most clearly inspired by the work of Donald Davidson.

Cavell endorses a theory of meaning which is usually called ‘externalism’. Externalism claims that - as Putnam famously put it - ‘meaning just ain't in the head’. Meaning is out there in the world, and the external world enters radically and forcefully into our mental processes. Many forms of externalism have been promoted by philosophers. True to her object-relational colours, Cavell advances a Wittgensteinian version: meaning is a function of participating in a language community. She also uses Davidson's notion of ‘radical interpretation’ to illuminate psychoanalytic concepts of interpretation. Radical interpretation is the process of attributing mental states to another person. Essentially, Davidson argues that we attribute mental states in a rationality-maximising fashion. We make sense of others' behaviour by understanding it as a relatively coherent whole. This leads to a third major philosophical doctrine: meaning holism. According to the theory of meaning holism, the meaning of an idea does not exist in isolation. The meaning of an idea is a function of how it fits into the whole fabric of a person's ideas. Every bit of the mind is intimately related to every other bit.

A second area of philosophical concern to Cavell deals with reasons, causes and psychological laws. Wittgenstein established the orthodoxy that causal explanations are fundamentally different from reason explanations and inspired a generation of philosophers to criticise Freud's alleged philosophical naivety in confusing the two. In the early 1960's, however, Davidson was working away at undermining the plausibility of Wittgenstein's story. Today, most Anglo-American philosophers accept that rational (psychological) explanations are a special type of causal explanation. Acceptance of this does not necessarily commit one to the view that the mind is governed by strict psychological laws. Cavell approaches this issue from the vantage point of Davidson's concept of ‘anomalous monism’. The bones of Davidson's argument is that the holistic character of psychological discourse makes such laws impossible. We do not identify ideas in the same way that we identify a chemical element. The content of an idea is (according to the theory of meaning holism) a function of its position within a web of ideas, is (according to the notion of radical interpretation) discerned by understanding the patterns of a person's life, and is (according to externalism) strongly determined by its context. Strict laws cannot cope with such strangely constituted entities. Cavell offers interesting criticisms of Grunbaum, Freud and Schafer in light of these concepts.

Teaching Klein

Linda Buckingham

Linda Buckingham

31 Harvard Court, Honeybourne Road, London NW6 lHL

Linda Buckingham  

For the past few years one of London's psychotherapy training institutions has employed me to teach a ten-week series of seminars.

I thought I would write about the experience of teaching Klein and about the lessons I have learned in doing so. I hope this is not an exercise in teaching my grandmothers to suck eggs! Rather, with the growth of courses on psychotherapeutic work with children and the continued application of Klein's ideas to clinical practice, I felt my experience may be useful to budding teachers and to anyone who may be invited to teach Kleinian theory in training institutions.

Of all psycho-analytic theories, Kleinian theory seems to be the most difficult for students to swallow. For instance, Freud's, Jung's and Winnicott's ideas on infancy are usually received with more friendliness than are Klein's. The reasons are not hard to discern. Klein's descriptions of the early life of the infant are unsettling and disturbing, especially the passage from the persecution, fragmentation and swings between contentment and hatred of the paranoid-schizoid position to the dawning of guilt and painful concern of the depressive position. The disturbing minutiae of Klein's descriptions combined with her rather bald, remorseless style leave many new readers of Klein reeling from the impact. ‘Surely babies don't suffer like this!’ students say, then demand how we can know about the content of early experience. Students who have had experience of infant observation find these questions easier to deal with, and for them the experience of reading Klein can be tempered and fleshed out by their observations. But reading Klein without parallel infant observation is, initially, a difficult business and feels persecutory, especially to students with young babies.

Though groups of students vary in their theoretical sophistication, their clinical experience and the dynamics peculiar to each group, I have found that teaching Klein goes through two distinct phases.

Phase One: Interest, Scepticism, Hostility

Interest

Klein's ideas always excite interest. Whatever one thinks of her style of writing her ideas burst from the page with vigour. They either resonate meaningfully or provoke distress, strong disagreement or other unsettled states of mind. I have never found anyone reacting to her work with indifference.

From Emptiness to Loss: A Journey from the Intrapersonal to the Interpersonal

Michael Lamprell

Michael Lamprell

36 Richmond Road, Leytonstone, London E11 4BU

Michael Lamprell  

In this paper the writer follows the changing meaning of the word ‘emptiness’ used by a patient in her therapy over a period of several years. He finds that it is possible to witness the journey in the therapy from a state of not-being, described as ‘emptiness’ at the beginning of the therapy, towards a feeling of loss, later in the therapy, when ‘emptiness’ takes on a new meaning. This journey can be seen to be linked with a developmental process from a perception of omnipotence and fusion towards a feeling of being separate.

The Patient and the Analyst: the basis of the psychoanalytic process by Joseph Sandler, Christopher Dare and Alex Holder, revised and expanded by Joseph Sandler and Anna Ursula Dreher. Published by Karnac Books, London, 1992; 238 pages; £14.95 (paperback).

Susan Budd

Susan Budd

London

Susan Budd  

This is a revised and enlarged edition of a textbook which first appeared in 1973, published by Allen and Unwin, and then was reprinted every three years from 1979 onward by Karnac. Its steady reprinting, and now its reissue, testify to its usefulness. Professor Sandler has argued for many years that much of the confusion and antagonism between rival versions of psychoanalytic theory could be clarified, and even cleared up, by a steady attention to the shifting meanings of the terms which are used. This is a familiar problem in all disciplines which develop a specialised vocabulary; it is exacerbated in those areas which lie very near to our most deeply-felt beliefs and experience.

Many of the concepts in psychoanalysis were first coined by Freud; interested in and sensitive as he was to problems of metapsychology and of meaning, he was more interested in trying to pin down his changing thoughts and ideas as they occurred to him, and as they were altered by his changing conceptions of the psyche. Two sources of confusion were immediately added. The first was the problem of translation. It is notorious that his English translators used Latinate terms instead of his more everyday German, trying to separate his concepts from concrete experience and give them a more impressive medical gloss. But we cannot simply reverse this by re-translating Freud. Other authors have used his concepts, as he intended them or as they understood them, and traditions of thought have branched off from them; it is as if we tried to get a tree to grow straight by cutting off most of its branches and twigs, taking with them the flowers and fruit. The Strachey et al translation of Freud was to have great influence, partly because it was excellently executed, early and in full, partly simply because more psychoanalysts, like doctors, engineers or any other professional group, speak English as a first or second language than any other.

Generations of analysts have used concepts such as the ‘ego’, each of them taking off from the point that the concept had reached when they were learning about it. Within less than a hundred years, different traditions of psychoanalytic discourse had developed within each of the countries to which ‘the plague’ had been spread; and as is notorious, when analysts from Vienna and Berlin were forced to emigrate, they found that psychoanalysis had developed different variants in its transplantation. Debates over which was ‘correct’, which was a fruitful development, which was a deviation, split the movement inside each country into separate tendencies. The authors argue that much of this could have been avoided if there had not been such a tendency to reify terminology. However, what Professor Sandler and his collaborators are doing is not establishing a glossary, but looking at how the concepts have been used, and what problems have been encountered in applying them in the analytic situation which has caused them to bend and shift and acquire new extensions. The literature that they have reviewed is predominantly that published in England and the United States; there is an excellent full bibliography of nearly five hundred items.

The Harvard Lectures by Anna Freud. Published by Karnac, London; 1992; 142 pages; £ 10.95.

Clifford Yorke

Clifford Yorke

South Moreton

Clifford Yorke  

Over forty years ago Anna Freud gave a series of nine lectures on psychoanalysis at Harvard University. There is no evidence that these were prepared except in her head, and it seems likely - as was often the case - that she did not speak from notes. They were, however, recorded on tape and later copied on cassettes, and it is these that have been transcribed to form the present book. Professor Joseph Sandler has edited them with care and skill, and Talcott Parsons, Chairman of the Department of Social Relations at Harvard, provides an introduction. The whole publishing enterprise is very worth while.

The lectures retain the liveliness and freshness that characterised Anna Freud's spoken talks, and in spite of the lapse of time give a remarkably succinct and impressive picture of classical psychoanalytis. There have of course been many developments within the classical framework since these lecture were given, particularly in the field of child development; but the lectures have lost none of their force as an introduction to the field. They cover in admirably lucid fashion all the basic psychoanalytic concepts, and will appeal not only to those coming to the subject for the very first time but provide a compact yet remarkably comprehensive refresher course for those looking for a review of basic classical principles.

Anna Freud started her professional life as a teacher, and a teacher she always remained. The publication of these lectures is a lasting reminder of an inimitable and engaging style that captivated with a deceptive but telling simplicity.

Psychotherapy in the General Practice Surgery: Working with and without a Secure Therapeutic Frame

John Launer

John Launer

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

John Launer  

Many general practices employ psychotherapists and counsellors. Some GPs have also had personal therapy and may have training in counselling or various therapies. Where different approaches are used, conflicts and rivalries can arise. This paper describes a flexible model which has helped one practice negotiate these issues. The model permits several levels of work: from opportunistic counselling in ordinary GP surgeries, to formal ‘secure-frame’ psychotherapy. The model allows patients and practitioners to sculpt their own experiences of counselling and therapy from a variety of approaches, and allows us to combine therapeutic work with medical practice.

Jan Wiener  

I think that most Jungians, particularly those in England, would agree that Michael Fordham has made some of the most original contributions to analytical psychology over the past fifty years. His interest in children and his firm conviction that we must understand the self in childhood have led to important new theoretical developments in our field. This memoir, written when Fordham was eighty-eight, makes easy and fascinating reading. I found it difficult to put down. This said, it has not been an easy book to review as the very act of reviewing seems like an intrusion into Fordham's very personal account of his life and work and the influences on them. I have comforted myself with the thought that it has probably been easier for me than it might have been for others. Whilst profoundly influenced by Fordham's writings, I do not know him well as a person, so bring fewer preconceptions or prejudices than those of the older generation who would have worked with him more closely.

Rob Weatherill

22 Pine Court, Blackrock, Co. Dublin, Eire

Rob Weatherill  

Psychoanalysis exists! It exists despite splitting attacks made on it by the analysand, and by the analyst's own internal objects, which threaten to destroy it. But it is the silent abundant goodness of the analytic setting, its freedom, its openness, its ‘without memory or desire’, that enable us to experience primary hate in face of terror. But no one possesses this goodness. Unless the analyst has some acknowledged or unacknowledged faith in this goodness, which is never his own, he will not be able to bear envy and will resort to cynicism or manipulation.

Castration Desire

David Mann

David Mann

Flat 6, 164 Lordship Road, London N16 5HB

David Mann  

This paper introduces the idea of castration desire: the desire to lose the penis to strengthen identification with the mother, to deny difference and thereby maintain the phantasy of fusion. Castration desire is therefore linked to the regressive part of the personality that seeks to avoid differentiation. In this context, castration anxiety is seen as a later development that actively promotes separation and individuation from the mother. These issues are explored using clinical and mythological examples.

The Psychoses: The Seminar of Jacques Lacan. Book 111 1955-1956 edited by Jacques-Alain Miller. Translated with notes by Russell Grigg. Published by Routledge, London, 1993; 341 pages; £14.99.

Bice Benvenuto

Bice Benvenuto

London

Bice Benvenuto  

With the 1955/56 seminar The Psychoses we come to the third year of Lacan's twenty-seven years of seminars given in Paris between 1953 and 1980 (year of his death). Lacan's teaching was an oral one based on these weekly seminars which some of his students transcribed over the years. Before his death, Lacan allowed his son-inlaw, Jacques-Alain Miller, to edit and publish some of the seminars, and left him the depository of his posthumous work. The third volume on psychosis came out one year after Lacan's death. So far only eight seminars have been published in France and only four in England.

Lacan was at his best with the spoken word, with its freshness, detours, flows and failings. He believed in the flying word, the one which cannot be frozen or stuck in an indelible writing - even though he published the Ecrits (Writings) in 1966, his most indecipherable text. Whereas writing fixes meaning, the spoken word lets meaning flow freely - free association. (For Freud the power of speech is the ‘talking cure’.) Lacan puts forward the hypothesis of the fundamental nature of words (signifiers) for the human mind: what is specific to human beings is the fact that they speak, and ‘Psychoanalysis is the science of language inhabited by the subject’. The question then arises: is the psychotic, like the neurotic, an inhabitant of language? Lacan comes to the conclusion that the psychotic does not inhabit, but is inhabited by, language; the phenomenon of auditory hallucinations bears witness to the fact that the psychotic is literally possessed by it. Through his reading of Schreber's written ‘memoirs’ Lacan unravels the thread by means of which Freud follows this case of paranoia: the threat of language, Schreber's tormenting voices which take over his existence: his psychosis speaks. Freud did not have Schreber on his couch but his Ariadne's thread for the reconstruction of Schreber's delusional system was to follow the thread of his written words. Schreber hears his own speech outside himself as coming from an immaterial ‘other’: the voices. And here Lacan points out the difference between his views on psychosis and those of the object-relations theorists. He refers to Ida MacAlpine's commentary on Schreber's case in the Standard Edition of Freud's work. MacAlpine situates paranoia within pre-oedipal phantasies and projections. But, Lacan argues, Freud had already corrected this view by stating that projection cannot explain delusion: neurotic projective proliferation and psychotic delusions cannot be confused.

John Bowlby and Attachment Theory by Jeremy Holmes. Published by Routledge, London, 1993; 249 pages.

John Southgate

John Southgate

London

John Southgate  

In the last issue of this Journal, Martin Stanton argued that if psychoanalysis and psychotherapy are to develop in the universities there will have to be a critical and comparative examination of all its hypotheses and theories as with all other subjects. In the same issue Jeremy Holmes informed us about a new development in the USA where a group of psychoanalysts have set up an Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis because the American Psychoanalytic Association does not want to ‘widen the narrow cannon of psychoanalytic authors deemed suitable for study, especially Bowlby, Kohut and Lacan’. Jeremy Holmes has himself contributed to this widening of general psychoanalytic developments by writing this book about John Bowlby and attachment theory.

In a way you get two books in one because there is a biography of John Bowlby presented along with an introduction to the many facets of attachment theory both in research and clinical terms. There are also useful clinical examples drawn from Jeremy Holmes' work as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and psychiatrist. Important contemporary research brings the reader up to date on this explaining field. The classic Bowlby work, such as that on maternal deprivation, attachment, loss, anger and grief, is combined with recent advances in child development research (‘post-Bowlbyan research’). Finally the implications for psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, psychiatry and society are described in four chapters.

The final chapter takes the form of a letter to John Bowlby because the author feels that writing a biography is also like a therapeutic relationship and the letter is to say goodbye. Jeremy Holmes comments that some people may have seen Bowlby as reserved, detached or even arrogant. My experience of being supervised by John Bowlby was that he was warm, friendly, intensely curious and provided me with a very secure base for my work. He was also, incidentally, able to apply attachment thinking to the problems of child abuse even though this was a new field for him.

Clinical Commentary XVI

[The material was sent ‘blind’ to three clinicians who were asked to comment on the session and on how their way of thinking about the patient would inform their way of working with him. Although the tradition of the Journal has been that commentators gave their theoretical orientation, I have found increasingly that they do not wish to be assigned to any ‘group’, let alone to be seen as representative of a group. This seems to be a trend across the institutions. M.B.]

The Therapist Writes

The History

The patient is a man in his early thirties, the third child after a gap of seven years of a professional couple. He studied chemistry at university and was expected to have a brilliant career. He hoped to obtain a research post in a good university department after he had completed his doctoral thesis but this did not materialise. He works in the research department of a specialist chemicals manufacturing firm. He feels the job is beneath him. Three years ago he married a woman a few years older than himself who is very successful as an agent in a branch of the entertainment world. She earns rather more than he does. There are no children; in fact, the marriage is virtually at an end since she has moved out and is living with a female friend. His childhood was apparently untraumatic, his parents are still very much in touch with him and helpful, but he felt his mother did not know what to do with him when he was a child. He was often sent to residential holiday schemes during the school holidays which he said he enjoyed.

He sought therapy because of his pervading sense of failure, difficulties in making relationships and sexual difficulties. I have been seeing this patient for two years thrice weekly. He is regular in his attendance although he frequently arrives late, sometimes as much as twenty minutes late.

He had considerable difficulty in associating and experiencing any significance in the experiences he described to me, which he tended to recount and then dismiss. There were long periods of time in the first six months when he talked, explained, theorised. I made interpretations without much confidence in my ability to touch him and he either accepted them politely or turned them down, sometimes politely, sometimes with contempt, and often as though they were simply an interruption in his chain of thought. References of mine to childhood incidents were often met with a comment like ‘I suppose it's your technique’ or ‘I gather you are interested in my mother’.

The Dream Discourse Today edited and introduced by Sara Flanders. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 1993; 256 pages; £35.00 (hardback), £14.99 (paperback)

Stephen Haine

Stephen Haine

London

Stephen Haine  

The Dream Discourse Today is one of the more recent additions to the New Library of Psychoanalysis, the series begun in 1987 by Routledge in association with the Institute of Psycho-Analysis in London. It is a series that is intended to create a greater appreciation of what psychoanalysis is really about. Sara Flanders is a practising psychoanalyst and for this book she has selected thirteen papers published in various psychoanalytic journals since 1962. To them she adds an introduction for the whole book - essentially a review of the place of dream in psychoanalytic thinking since Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) - and then a brief introduction to each of the four sections she has constructed.

Going through the book I came to realise what a complex and rather difficult task she had undertaken. It is a task which she has done, I believe, admirably. To present something reasonably coherent about dreams to an outside world, when the psychoanalytic world is marked and sometimes riven by difference, is no mean feat. To achieve this Flanders adopts a strictly non-committal line, attempting to select judiciously, record accurately and balance fairly material from various directions (historical, north American, European, Freudian, Kleinian, Independent perspectives and traditions). While allowing the reader to make up his/her own mind she also tacitly maintains the line that such differences are evolutionary and essentially creative. Some might see this as a little presumptuous or over optimistic; but she is persuasive.

My guess is that the book will appeal beyond the psychoanalytic psychotherapeutic world to people from the other disciplines that Routledge list - history, linguistics, literature, medicine, philosophy, psychology and the social sciences - though I may be misjudging the sophistication and level of interest of non-analytic readers. Certainly there is a nice combination of concise description and analytic map-making in her introduction that sets the scene for analytic and non-analytic readers alike. But I do not know how widespread the interest is among other disciplines in, for example, the classical ‘dream controversy’ - essentially the question of uniqueness of dream. This Flanders introduces with papers by Charles Brenner and Ralph Greenson, Brenner arguing that the dream is no more ‘special’ than jokes, symptoms and suchlike, all of them being informed by phantasy and illustrative of the workings of the unconscious mind; Greenson per contra arguing for the uniqueness of dream, the royal road. One hopes that this is a debate that is alive for practising therapists and it is useful to have these papers opposed. But for the non-analyst…1 am less sure.

[[RunningHead]]

Coups d'Etat and Catastrophic Change: Shakespeare's Julius Caesar**

Margaret and Michael Rustin

Michael Rustin

Faculty of Social Sciences, University of East London, Longbridge Road, Dagenham RM8 2AS

Michael Rustin  

Miscommunication, both in the form of deception and self-deception, is endemic in the action of Shakespeare's Julius Caesar. This article investigates why this should be, and links the functions of miscommunication in the play with its psychoanalytic meanings as these have been outlined in particular by Bion. The truth is avoided or manipulated by most of the protagonists of the play as a response to their anxieties about catastrophic change. The fear of the conspirators that Caesar is about to accept a crown is only the focal point of a deeper anxiety about the threat to the Roman republic. The play is shown to illuminate unconscious forces involved in political leadership and mass politics in particular. The preparation and enactment of the assassination add a burden of failed mourning and of unassimilable guilt to already deep anxieties, all of which lead to the cumulative tragedies which the play depicts.

Maggie Fagan  

This eloquent book, a collection of papers, concentrates on the pivotal events of a woman's lifecycle - adolescence, pregnancy, childbirth, the menopause and old age. It looks at the psychological tasks precipitated by these events - or their absence as in the case of infertility - and, by including a wealth of case studies, it illustrates how individual women have come to terms with their biological reality.

From the outset the book is distinguished by its fluency and subtlety as it details the complex interplay between external and internal reality. Such is the eloquence of Dr Pines’ writing in the introduction, where she puts together her own family circumstances and historical events after the Second World War, that I found myself regretting that this book wasn't to continue as an autobiography. But then perhaps there is something autobiographical in these essays, expressed in the obvious empathy Dr Pines has for her patients and her deep interest in the life cycle, the continuation of which has such importance for an optimistic and reparative view of life.

The book's predominant theme - how women learn to translate psychic pain into physical suffering in an attempt to bypass the psychic process of suffering intolerable pain - is introduced in the first paper, ‘Skin communication’. Dr Pines concludes that women who suffered from infantile eczema may have experienced a fundamental disturbance in the mother-infant relationship and that these women unconsciously attempt to find, and long for, experiences in adult life where they are bodily soothed.

The next papers form a group exploring the issues of pregnancy, childbirth, miscarriage and abortion, with an emphasis on the importance of identification. Two identifications are concentrated upon: as a pregnant woman identifies with her own mother, and therefore with the wish to become a mother to a baby, she also feels identified with the foetus, which naturally intensifies the universal infantile wish to be mothered again. Consequently, Dr Pines argues, pregnancy necessarily involves psychic conflict. In ‘Adolescent pregnancy and motherhood’ and in ‘Pregnancy, miscarriage and abortion’, Dr Pines explores the issues of identification based on early psychic experience and it is in the latter paper that most of her ideas are best presented.

Laurie Wright

Laurie Wright

Canterbury

Laurie Wright  

Over the past two decades there has been an enormous growth in the interest and publication of literature on the subject of childhood sexual abuse. Using the American Psychological Association's abstracting service, Psychlit disc, with the key phrase sexual abuse I found a listing of 216 journal articles published between the years 1974 and 1986. Accessing the second file of this service, which covers the years between 1987 and 1994, the service shows a huge increase in publications to a total of 2166 articles on sexual abuse. Additionally it shows 736 books or chapters dedicated to the topic. Clearly clinicians and survivors alike are swimming in a sea of theory and advice. This growth seems to me not only indicative of a growing patient population, but also of the sense of bewilderment felt throughout the profession in reference to working sensitively and ethically with this patient population. When Davies and Frawley's book came to my attention, my first thought was to question what could they possibly offer that has not already been published? But their subtitle A Psychoanalytic Perspective held out the promise of something consolidating and new in the literature on this subject.

Within the introduction they draw their lines of theoretical influence. Beginning with a discussion of Freud's abandonment of the seduction theory, they move on to build their model clearly within a relational perspective. Their knowledge of theory is scholarly and encyclopaedic as they sweep through theoreticians making compatible use of an Anglo-American consortium as diverse as Kohut and Sullivan from the American schools, and Fairbairn and Winnicott from the British schools. Their model is impressive, well articulated and applicable, if at times running the risk of being overwhelmingly theoretical. (In one paragraph alone they cite twenty-four references!)

Central to their theory is an emphasis on the clinician's need to understand the process of dissociation when working with survivors of childhood trauma, and particularly its application to work with survivors of sexual abuse. Using Kohut's model of a vertical split within psychic structure they describe work with survivors as feeling analogous to working simultaneously with two patients.

Its pages reveal the journey of a well-seasoned traveller of both the internal and external world, who generously shares her humanity, humour and dedication. Nina Coltart's conversational and untheoretical style invites you to take a friendly stroll. Perhaps this is why areas of controversy are only obliquely referred to.

Most people who have trained with one of the London analytic psychotherapy organisations within the last couple of decades will certainly know or know of Dr Coltart. She has become very much a mother/grandmother figure to generations of psychotherapists whom she advised, supervised, encouraged, referred on to training therapists and referred patients to. A common sense approach has typified her stance and permeates the pages of this book.

In the Introduction Nina Coltart distinguishes between survival ‘in its rawest bleakest sense’ and survival in its positive sense (p. 1):

At the heart of the matter lies the idea of enjoyment: enjoyment of the experience which is being survived, and enjoyment of the ways in which it enriches the whole of the life of the survivor, whether working or relaxing, or simply being oneself.

This latter use of the word survival in relation to enjoyment will resonate with many of us familiar with the work of Winnicott, who refers to the survival of the object as being of paramount importance in the patient/analyst relationship. What the reader will find here is advice on how the therapist must provide for herself. This is what is refreshing and unusual. Instead of a treatise on what we must do for our patients the implication throughout is that we can be nothing for our patients if we do not tend to our own needs and desires. It is true that the emphasis in all training organisations is the trainee's personal therapy, but it is as if that's supposed to take care of everything. Consequently a great deal can too easily get taken for granted about the practical details of becoming a psychotherapist. The practicalities Dr Coltart addresses fill a gap in our literature.
